decisions.title: Cognitive lifecycle state machine is the authoritative orchestration model

context.problem: The system contains multiple cognitive modes and transitions, but no recorded ADR explains why the lifecycle exists or what invariants future changes must preserve.
constraints: Cognitive operations are stateful and may have long-running side effects
Dreaming, normalization, lucid exploration, nightmare scanning, and discipline ingest must remain distinguishable
Future changes by humans or agents need guard rails to avoid invalid state transitions

decision.chosen: Treat the explicit cognitive lifecycle states (including AWAKE, REM, NORMALIZING, NIGHTMARE, LUCID, and INGEST) as the authoritative orchestration model. New cognitive actions must either map onto an existing lifecycle state or extend the lifecycle with a reviewed ADR.

alternatives.option: Use ad hoc booleans and per-feature execution flags
alternatives.rejected_because: This would fragment orchestration logic and make transition safety unverifiable.

alternatives.option: Collapse all non-awake behavior into a single background state
alternatives.rejected_because: This would erase important semantic differences between dreaming, normalization, adversarial scanning, and interactive lucid investigation.

expected: State transitions become a protected architectural seam
Tooling and docs can reason consistently about system behavior
New cognitive features must explicitly define how they enter and leave lifecycle states
risks: The lifecycle may feel heavyweight for experimental features
Adding new states requires deliberate governance

guard_rails: Do NOT add a new cognitive execution mode without mapping it to the lifecycle or recording a replacement ADR.
Do NOT bypass lifecycle transitions in tooling or extension integrations.
Do NOT merge lifecycle states solely for implementation convenience without reviewing downstream tool and prompt impacts.

decisions.title: Discipline sessions are mandatory governance for risky code modification workflows

context.problem: The repository includes a discipline subsystem, but there is no ADR documenting why modification tasks should be structured into evidence-backed phases with write protections.
constraints: The project is modified by humans and agents
Some tools can write source files and persistent knowledge
Ground-truth evidence is required before proposing or executing changes
Future contributors need clear expectations about when planning and verification are mandatory

decision.chosen: Use discipline sessions as the default governance mechanism for audits, ports, reconstructions, and non-trivial modifications. Evidence collection in INGEST/AUDIT, explicit planning, and post-change verification are the intended operating model for risky changes.

alternatives.option: Allow free-form modification without phase gating
alternatives.rejected_because: This increases the risk of unsupported claims, unsafe writes, and silent regressions.

alternatives.option: Use discipline only for external contributors
alternatives.rejected_because: Internal and agent-driven changes have the same need for traceable evidence and guarded execution.

expected: Safer write operations and better auditability
Improved reproducibility of agent-assisted changes
More explicit link between source-of-truth evidence and implemented diffs
risks: The workflow adds overhead for small changes
Tooling bugs in the discipline layer can block legitimate work

guard_rails: Do NOT weaken evidence requirements for risky code changes without a replacement governance mechanism.
Do NOT permit protected writes in modification workflows without an approved plan or equivalent explicit review policy.
Do NOT remove verification expectations for changes that alter behavior, persistence, or user-visible flows.

decisions.title: VS Code extension and backend communicate through an explicit, versioned contract

context.problem: The extension depends on backend/daemon behavior, but there is no ADR defining the trust boundary, failure handling expectations, or compatibility contract between the VS Code client and DreamGraph services.
constraints: The extension must remain usable when backend services are degraded or unavailable
Webview and extension-host state can diverge if contracts are implicit
The project may evolve backend APIs and extension UX independently

decision.chosen: Treat the VS Code extension ↔ backend interface as an explicit contract. Requests and responses should be versionable, capability-aware where needed, and designed for graceful degradation when the backend is unavailable.

alternatives.option: Rely on informal coupling between current extension code and server implementation
alternatives.rejected_because: This increases breakage risk and makes compatibility failures hard to diagnose.

alternatives.option: Push all state into the webview and use the extension host as a thin proxy
alternatives.rejected_because: This weakens host-side control over persistence, recovery, and instance-aware orchestration.

expected: Backend changes become easier to reason about and stage
The extension can implement clearer degraded/offline UX
State ownership remains concentrated in the extension host rather than fragmented in the webview
risks: Versioning introduces some protocol maintenance overhead
Capability mismatches need to be surfaced intentionally

guard_rails: Do NOT introduce breaking extension/backend message changes without a versioning or compatibility story.
Do NOT make the webview the sole source of truth for persistent chat or instance state.
Do NOT assume backend availability in user-facing extension flows without a degraded-mode response.

decisions.title: Chat conversation state in the VS Code extension is owned by the extension host and must survive webview recreation

context.problem: The chat UI can be torn down when users switch away and return, causing user-visible loss of conversation content if state depends on transient webview DOM state.
constraints: VS Code webviews may be hidden and recreated by the host
Users expect chat continuity within a workspace and instance
The extension already includes chat memory facilities and instance-aware behavior

decision.chosen: Keep the extension host as the authoritative owner of chat state and rehydrate any recreated or re-shown webview from host-held memory. Persist conversation history per DreamGraph instance so view switches and panel recreation do not erase the chat transcript.

alternatives.option: Store chat transcript only in the webview DOM or JavaScript runtime
alternatives.rejected_because: This state is lost when the webview is disposed or reloaded.

alternatives.option: Treat each chat panel reveal as a fresh session
alternatives.rejected_because: This breaks conversational continuity and frustrates users.

expected: Switching tabs/views will no longer erase the chat history
Extension-host logic remains the single source of truth for message history
Instance-aware chat restoration becomes deterministic
risks: Persisted history may need pruning or explicit clearing UX
Hydration logic must avoid duplicate rendering when panels are revived

guard_rails: Do NOT rely on transient webview memory as the only storage for chat transcript state.
Do NOT clear host-side chat state merely because the panel is hidden or recreated.
Do NOT add a second authoritative transcript store without defining reconciliation rules.

decisions.title: Architect chat must use structured tool-calling rather than stream-only narration

context.problem: The VS Code architect chat panel delegated tool-capable requests to a placeholder that only streamed plain text. Because tool schemas were not sent to the provider API, the model narrated tool invocations as text/JSON instead of executing them, severing all MCP and local tool workflows.
constraints: The VS Code architect must support both MCP tools and local extension tools
Provider support must work across Anthropic and OpenAI-style tool-calling APIs
Tool execution state must be represented as iterative assistant tool_use and user tool_result turns
The extension must remain within the project workspace boundary and use existing local tool dispatch for filesystem and command execution

decision.chosen: Replace the stream-only placeholder path with a real iterative agentic loop that calls callWithTools, dispatches local or MCP tools based on the tool name, accumulates raw tool_use/tool_result messages, and continues until a non-tool final response is returned.

alternatives.option: Keep plain streaming and describe tools in prompt only
alternatives.rejected_because: This reproduces the failure mode where the model narrates intended actions without structured tool execution.

alternatives.option: Implement provider-specific tool loops directly in the chat panel without using architect-llm callWithTools
alternatives.rejected_because: This would duplicate logic already implemented in architect-llm and weaken cross-provider consistency.

expected: Architect responses can execute local and MCP tools instead of narrating them
File creation and other action-oriented tasks become achievable through the chat UI
Raw provider message translation remains centralized in architect-llm
Future tool failures can be debugged at the orchestration boundary with clearer provenance
risks: Iterative tool loops can create runaway execution if stop reasons are mishandled
Provider raw-message translation bugs can still cause partial failures
Tool result handling remains sensitive to malformed tool outputs

guard_rails: Do NOT route tool-capable architect requests through stream-only code paths.
Do NOT bypass architect-llm callWithTools when structured tool execution is required.
Do NOT replace iterative tool_use/tool_result accumulation with prompt-only descriptions of tool availability.

decisions.title: Preserve end-to-end agentic tool execution loop in VS Code chat panel

context.problem: The VS Code chat experience could narrate intended tool use without actually executing tools when the chat panel streamed placeholder text instead of running the architect LLM tool loop. This severed the end-to-end loop between model-emitted tool_use instructions and actual local/MCP tool execution, producing false success narratives and unreliable operational behavior.
constraints: All tool-capable chat responses must route through the architect LLM tool orchestration path rather than a placeholder streaming path.
The chat panel must preserve iterative execution semantics: model emits tool_use -> system executes tool -> tool_result is appended -> model continues until final answer.
Both MCP tools and local support tools are part of the supported execution surface and must remain invocable from the same loop.
User-visible success claims must be grounded in actual executed tool results, not inferred intent or narrated plans.
Changes must stay within the VS Code extension project boundary and avoid direct mutation of protected graph data outside approved MCP tools.

decision.chosen: The VS Code chat panel must use the architect LLM's tool-capable call path as the authoritative execution mechanism for chat interactions that may invoke tools. The system must maintain a closed-loop agentic workflow: gather tool definitions, invoke callWithTools, detect tool_use outputs, dispatch each tool call to the appropriate executor (local support tool or MCP tool), append structured tool_result messages, and continue iterating until the model returns a final answer without pending tool calls.

alternatives.option: Keep placeholder stream()-based chat rendering and treat tool mentions as informational only
alternatives.rejected_because: This creates a misleading user experience where the assistant appears to act without executing tools, breaking trust and preventing real orchestration.

alternatives.option: Allow separate ad hoc execution paths for local tools and MCP tools
alternatives.rejected_because: Multiple execution paths increase drift risk, make verification harder, and can break the required tool_result continuation semantics.

alternatives.option: Rely on manual operator verification instead of enforcing execution-loop integrity in code
alternatives.rejected_because: Manual verification can catch regressions after the fact but does not prevent false success claims or broken automation at runtime.

expected: Chat responses that mention tool activity will be backed by actual tool executions.
The architect LLM layer remains the single authoritative translation point for provider-specific tool-call formats.
Future regressions are easier to detect because the execution chain is conceptually explicit: tool_use -> execute -> tool_result -> continue.
The extension can safely support mixed local and MCP orchestration in one conversation loop.
risks: The iterative tool loop is more complex than a plain streaming response path and may regress if refactored without preserving stop-reason handling.
Provider-specific response-shape changes could break tool_use detection unless translation remains maintained.
Error handling or rate-limit behavior may still cause partial executions if not surfaced clearly to the user.

guard_rails: Do NOT replace the chat panel's tool-capable execution path with a placeholder or display-only streaming path for interactions that may invoke tools.
Do NOT claim that a tool action succeeded unless a corresponding tool execution result was actually received and incorporated into the conversation.
Do NOT split local-tool and MCP-tool orchestration into incompatible loops that bypass the shared tool_result continuation mechanism.
Do NOT modify architect tool-call translation behavior without validating that emitted tool_use events still reach the chat-panel execution loop end-to-end.

decisions.title: Canonical Feature Identity Uses feature_* IDs

context.problem: The fact graph contains duplicate and legacy feature identities for the same architectural areas, especially dashboard and VS Code extension surfaces (for example feature_dashboard_server vs dashboard/dashboard_server and feature_vscode_extension vs vscode_extension/extensions_vscode). This fragments ownership, weakens UI registry used_by mappings, and makes graph queries ambiguous.
constraints: Must preserve existing graph data without destructive deletion
UI registry ownership should resolve to stable feature IDs
Changes must remain within existing DreamGraph feature/data protection model
No accepted ADR currently defines canonical naming for feature identities

decision.chosen: Use feature_* IDs as the canonical identity scheme for authoritative feature entities. Legacy non-canonical feature entries may remain temporarily for historical continuity, but all new enrichment and UI registry used_by mappings must target canonical feature_* IDs. Consolidation work should strengthen canonical entries and mark legacy aliases as superseded in descriptions/metadata rather than relying on them for ownership.

alternatives.option: Keep mixed historical IDs indefinitely
alternatives.rejected_because: Leaves graph queries ambiguous and preserves fragmented ownership semantics.

alternatives.option: Delete legacy feature entries immediately
alternatives.rejected_because: Higher risk because other graph references may still point at those IDs and DreamGraph lacks a dedicated feature-delete/supersede flow.

alternatives.option: Use source-path-derived IDs as canonical feature identifiers
alternatives.rejected_because: Would be less stable for conceptual features spanning multiple files and UIs.

expected: UI registry ownership becomes consistent across dashboard and extension surfaces
Future enrichment converges on stable canonical feature identifiers
Legacy aliases can still be discovered during transition but should no longer own semantics
risks: Some existing queries may still return legacy features until broader cleanup is complete
Without a dedicated deprecation mechanism for features, legacy nodes remain visible and may confuse users temporarily

guard_rails: Do NOT introduce new authoritative feature entities for existing capabilities unless they follow the feature_* canonical ID scheme.
Do NOT register UI used_by ownership against legacy aliases when a canonical feature_* entity already exists.
Do NOT treat dashboard, dashboard_server, server_dashboard, vscode_extension, or extensions_vscode as authoritative owners while canonical feature_* entries exist.

decisions.title: Semantic UI Registry Includes Abstract Visual Language and Layout Contracts

context.problem: The current semantic UI registry captures purpose, data contracts, interactions, implementations, and ownership, but it under-specifies visual styling and layout characteristics that are architecturally important for preserving consistent UX across dashboard and extension surfaces. Without abstract visual metadata, the registry cannot fully describe composition intent, emphasis hierarchy, spacing density, navigation chrome, or state-driven styling while remaining platform-agnostic.
constraints: UI registry must remain semantic and platform-agnostic rather than storing raw CSS or framework-specific style props.
Visual metadata must describe intent and layout contracts, not pixel-perfect implementation details.
Existing registered UI elements should remain valid and be enrichable incrementally.
Metadata should support both server-rendered dashboard HTML and VS Code extension surfaces.

decision.chosen: Extend the semantic UI registry convention to include abstract visual and layout metadata for UI elements. This metadata should describe visual role, density, emphasis, chrome level, layout pattern, alignment, hierarchy, responsive behavior, and state-driven styling semantics, while avoiding concrete CSS values or implementation-specific component props.

alternatives.option: Keep registry purely behavioral and omit visual/layout metadata
alternatives.rejected_because: Leaves an architectural blind spot where shared UX structure and visual intent are undocumented and hard to port or validate.

alternatives.option: Store raw CSS/design-token/framework style props directly in the registry
alternatives.rejected_because: Violates platform abstraction and would couple the registry to specific implementations rather than semantic intent.

expected: UI registry entries can better express cross-platform UX intent and composition rules.
Migration and reconstruction tasks can preserve layout and visual hierarchy more accurately.
Some existing UI elements will need incremental enrichment to adopt the expanded metadata model.
risks: Visual metadata may drift toward implementation detail if not governed carefully.
Different contributors may interpret abstract styling categories inconsistently until conventions stabilize.

guard_rails: Do NOT store raw CSS, Tailwind classes, or framework-specific style props as authoritative UI registry metadata.
Do NOT replace semantic purpose/data-contract metadata with purely visual descriptions; visual metadata is additive.

When registering or updating UI elements, prefer abstract layout and visual intent terms such as card grid, dense inspector, primary action emphasis, or embedded shell chrome over pixel-level specifications.

decisions.title: Canonical UI Registry Uses Semantic ui_* IDs and Transitional Legacy Entries

context.problem: The UI registry contains overlapping legacy and canonical entries for similar dashboard and extension surfaces, which causes exported docs and graph queries to mix authoritative semantic elements with older aliases or parallel representations.
constraints: Preserve backward compatibility for existing registry consumers and older references.
Do not delete legacy entries without a dedicated retirement mechanism.
Canonical entries must remain abstract and platform-independent.
Registry ownership should align with ADR-010 feature identity conventions.

decision.chosen: Treat semantically named ui_* entries and the established canonical dashboard/extension surfaces as authoritative. Legacy or parallel UI entries remain transitional references only and must not be preferred in new ownership mappings, new docs examples, or future enrichment passes.

alternatives.option: Delete duplicate legacy UI entries immediately
alternatives.rejected_because: There is no dedicated non-destructive retirement flow for UI elements, and immediate deletion risks breaking historical references.

alternatives.option: Keep enriching all legacy and canonical entries equally
alternatives.rejected_because: That would preserve ambiguity and continue to pollute the registry with overlapping authoritative representations.

expected: Future registry enrichment will target canonical ui_* entries first.
Exported docs can be interpreted with a clear distinction between canonical and transitional UI entities.
Ownership mappings and examples become more consistent across dashboard and extension surfaces.
risks: Legacy duplicate UI entries still remain queryable until a retirement mechanism exists.
Some consumers may still surface legacy entries unless additional filtering is added in docs or queries.

guard_rails: Do NOT create new authoritative UI registry entries for existing surfaces when a canonical ui_* entry already exists.
Do NOT prefer legacy or parallel non-canonical UI entries in used_by mappings, examples, or enrichment passes when a canonical entry exists.
Do NOT encode platform-specific styling tokens into canonical UI registry entries.

decisions.title: UI Registry Supports Backward-Compatible Retirement and Export Filtering

context.problem: The UI registry contained canonical ui_* entries alongside legacy or parallel entries. Without lifecycle metadata, exports and queries surfaced all entries equally, making the semantic inventory noisy and making canonicalization incomplete.
constraints: Must remain backward compatible with existing ui_registry.json data and register_ui_element payloads.
Must not delete historical UI entries destructively.
Canonical ui_* entries established by ADR-013 must remain authoritative.
Living docs should prefer active canonical entries while still preserving historical traceability.

decision.chosen: Add optional UI registry lifecycle fields (status, superseded_by, deprecation_reason). Treat omitted status as active for backward compatibility. Extend query/export behavior so deprecated entries can be filtered from primary views while still being documented as legacy references.

alternatives.option: Delete legacy UI entries outright
alternatives.rejected_because: Would lose historical traceability and risks breaking existing references.

alternatives.option: Keep legacy entries without lifecycle metadata
alternatives.rejected_because: Leaves canonicalization ambiguous and docs noisy.

expected: Canonical UI entries become easier to identify in queries and exports.
Legacy entries remain available for compatibility but no longer dominate primary documentation.
Future retirement of overlapping UI entries can be done non-destructively.
risks: Some existing exports may show newly added deprecated sections, changing documentation shape slightly.
Legacy entries without explicit superseded_by values would remain ambiguous until curated.

guard_rails: Do NOT require lifecycle fields on older UI registry entries; omitted status must continue to mean active.
Do NOT delete legacy UI entries when a non-destructive deprecated or transitional state is sufficient.
Do NOT include deprecated UI entries in primary migration planning by default.
Do NOT let deprecated legacy entries outrank canonical ui_* entries in exported documentation.

decisions.title: Data Storage Strategy

context.problem: To ensure efficient and reliable data management across the application.
constraints: Transactional data must be stored in a relational database
Configuration data must be stored in JSON files

decision.chosen: Use a relational database for transactional data and JSON files for configuration.

alternatives.option: Store all data in a NoSQL database
alternatives.rejected_because: Does not meet transactional consistency requirements.

alternatives.option: Use XML for configuration
alternatives.rejected_because: JSON is more lightweight and easier to parse.

expected: Improved data integrity and easier configuration management.
risks: Migration challenges if data storage strategy changes in the future.

guard_rails: Do NOT change data storage formats without reviewing this ADR.

decisions.title: Tension evidence must preserve semantic anchors as primary and treat line numbers as optional hints

context.problem: Long-lived tensions and cognitive evidence become brittle when preserved primarily as file line-number references. Source files evolve, causing line offsets to drift and weakening the durability and auditability of tension evidence across time, dream cycles, and repository changes.
constraints: Tension evidence must remain durable across routine source edits and refactors.
Cognitive artifacts need traceable provenance without depending on unstable positional coordinates.
Existing code references and line ranges remain useful for short-term inspection and debugging, but must not be treated as canonical long-lived evidence.
The evidence model should support future normalization, dream cycles, and cross-instance sharing without fragile source offsets.

decision.chosen: DreamGraph will preserve semantic evidence as the primary long-lived basis for tensions and cognitive insights. Canonical evidence should prefer semantic anchors such as entity names, feature IDs, workflow IDs, repository responsibilities, aggregate boundaries, save/sync behaviors, and relationship descriptions. File paths and line ranges may be stored only as optional cached hints for operator convenience and must not be required for the tension to remain meaningful or valid over time.

alternatives.option: Continue storing line-number references as primary evidence
alternatives.rejected_because: This makes long-lived tensions stale as files change and weakens durability across refactors.

alternatives.option: Remove source-code location references entirely
alternatives.rejected_because: Line hints and file references still help short-term inspection and debugging, so they remain useful as secondary evidence.

alternatives.option: Store only raw code excerpts as canonical evidence
alternatives.rejected_because: Raw excerpts drift too, are harder to normalize across instances, and are less queryable than semantic anchors.

expected: Tensions remain interpretable even after source files shift.
Cross-cycle and cross-instance cognitive evidence becomes more durable.
Operators can still navigate to file regions when hints are available, but evidence quality no longer depends on stable offsets.
Future graph tooling can prioritize semantic linking and entity-based provenance over positional references.
risks: Existing historical tensions may still contain fragile line-based evidence and need gradual normalization.
Some semantic anchors may be underspecified when the graph is sparse, requiring fallback hints until the graph is enriched.
Tooling may need follow-up updates to ensure new tensions are recorded with semantic-first evidence.

guard_rails: Do NOT treat file line numbers as the canonical long-lived identity or primary justification of a tension.
Do NOT discard semantic entity/workflow/behavior evidence in favor of positional references when both are available.
Do NOT require stable line offsets for a tension or cognitive insight to be considered valid over time.
If line numbers are stored, treat them as optional cached navigation hints only.

decisions.title: Semantic anchors are canonical; positional coordinates are advisory only

context.problem: Context anchoring based on line numbers, cursor positions, and offsets is brittle under edits, symbol movement, and refactors. The extension needs a stable identity model for evidence selection, packet rendering, and cross-session context reuse.
constraints: Coordinates can drift after edits and must not be treated as identity.
Anchor resolution must prefer semantic identifiers over positional hints.
VS Code symbol resolution is the primary local authority before heuristic fallback.
Legacy coordinate-based anchors must remain backward-compatible during migration.
Graph-backed canonical IDs should be used when available for promotion across features, workflows, ADRs, and UI elements.

decision.chosen: Semantic anchors are the canonical identity for context. Preferred anchor hierarchy is graph entity IDs, symbol names/paths, workflow IDs, ADR IDs, UI registry IDs, relationship assertions, and semantic fingerprints. Repository paths, file paths, and module/class names are secondary. Line numbers, cursor positions, offsets, and snippets are advisory only and may be used as hints but never as canonical identity.

alternatives.option: Continue treating line numbers and cursor positions as primary anchors
alternatives.rejected_because: High drift rate under edits and poor cross-session stability cause stale evidence binding and degraded retrieval precision.

alternatives.option: Use file paths plus line ranges as canonical identity
alternatives.rejected_because: More stable than raw coordinates but still breaks under symbol movement, file splits, and refactors; does not capture semantic sameness.

alternatives.option: Use heuristic/snippet-only anchoring
alternatives.rejected_because: Useful as fallback, but ambiguous, token-expensive, and weaker than symbol or graph identity.

expected: Reasoning packets become more resilient to edits and symbol relocation.
Stored anchors can be migrated by exact match, rebound on symbol moves, downgraded on drift, or archived when no match exists.
Evidence selection can prioritize relevance, confidence, token cost, and anchor relation using canonical anchors.
Rendered context will better communicate semantic identity and approximate matches.
risks: Symbol provider gaps or extraction misses may temporarily reduce anchor precision.
Promotion to graph-backed canonical IDs depends on graph freshness and may be incomplete in sparse areas.
Backward-compatible migration logic adds complexity during the transition period.

guard_rails: Do NOT treat line numbers, cursor positions, offsets, or snippets as canonical identity in new context-building logic.
Do NOT bypass VS Code symbol resolution when a symbol-aware anchor can be derived.
Do NOT introduce full-file-read-first anchoring as the default path; full file reads remain planner-authorized, debugging-only, or explicitly requested.
When a semantic anchor can be promoted to a graph-backed canonical ID, preserve that canonical identity through packet construction and rendering.
Legacy anchors from prior sessions must be migrated through exact match, rebind, drift downgrade, or archive logic rather than trusted as-is.

decisions.title: Two-pass graph context fetch with confidence-gated direct feature refinement

context.problem: File-path-only graph context retrieval produced useful but lower-confidence feature matches, while exact feature_id matches produced higher relevance. However, canonical feature IDs are not available until after Phase 3 anchor promotion, which occurs after the initial graph context fetch in ContextBuilder.buildEnvelope.
constraints: Keep all operations within the VS Code extension and DreamGraph daemon project boundary
Preserve existing one-round-trip behavior when no strong feature candidate exists
Avoid requiring full architectural reordering of buildEnvelope phases
Use daemon /api/graph-context exact feature_ids matching when a strong candidate is available
Retain backward-compatible fallback behavior if the second pass fails or returns no new data

decision.chosen: Use a two-pass graph context fetch inside _resolveGraphContext. Pass 1 always queries by file_path and evidence flags. Then a local confidence-gated pre-scorer evaluates Pass-1 features against the active anchor identity. When a candidate score is >= 0.75, Pass 2 re-queries /api/graph-context with feature_ids:[candidateId] to trigger the daemon's exact-match path and higher per-entity relevance. Merge Pass-2 entities into the existing graph context, de-duplicating by ID and upgrading relevance in place. If no strong candidate exists or Pass 2 fails, retain the Pass-1 result unchanged.

alternatives.option: Single-pass file_path-only retrieval
alternatives.rejected_because: It cannot reliably exploit exact feature_id matching, so relevance remains lower and less anchor-specific.

alternatives.option: Reorder buildEnvelope so Phase 3 promotion happens before graph fetch
alternatives.rejected_because: This would require broader architectural changes and promotion currently depends on graphContext candidates produced by the fetch itself.

alternatives.option: Always run a second graph-context fetch
alternatives.rejected_because: It adds unnecessary latency and cost on turns where no strong candidate exists.

expected: Higher feature relevance when the active anchor strongly maps to a returned feature
Improved downstream evidence ordering because aggregateRelevance can observe direct-match scores
No regression for weak or ambiguous anchors because the second pass is skipped
A small latency increase only on high-confidence turns that trigger Pass 2
risks: Threshold sensitivity may under-trigger or over-trigger the second pass until tuned
Future refactors may remove the second pass as redundant unless the rationale is preserved
Merge logic could drift if graph context entity shapes change without corresponding updates

guard_rails: Do NOT remove the confidence gate or unconditional fallback without re-evaluating latency versus relevance trade-offs
Do NOT replace the two-pass merge with an unconditional second fetch on every turn without revisiting this ADR
Do NOT assume canonical feature IDs are available before Phase 3 promotion unless buildEnvelope ordering is explicitly redesigned

decisions.title: ADR-003 through ADR-007 verified implementation anchors in current VS Code extension and orchestration surfaces

context.problem: ADR-003 through ADR-007 were already accepted, but the graph lacked durable implementation anchors showing where their guard rails are concretely enforced in the current codebase. Without recorded anchors, future reasoning could drift back to generic architectural summaries instead of verified code surfaces.
constraints: Must not alter the accepted meaning of ADR-003 through ADR-007
Anchors must use current verified implementation surfaces in the VS Code extension host and orchestration layer
Evidence must prefer semantic anchors over line numbers
Recorded knowledge must stay within existing project scope and repo surfaces

decision.chosen: Record a companion architecture decision that captures the verified implementation anchors for ADR-003 through ADR-007 in the current codebase. ADR-003 is anchored in extension.ts, McpClient, and HealthMonitor. ADR-004 is anchored in ChatMemory plus ChatPanel host-side message ownership and rehydration. ADR-005 is anchored in HealthMonitor and the extension reporting/request-budget instrumentation path. ADR-006 is anchored in ArchitectLlm.callWithTools with provider-native tool schema translation. ADR-007 is anchored in the ChatPanel iterative tool execution loop and tool-result reinjection path.

alternatives.option: Leave ADRs mapped only in transient chat history
alternatives.rejected_because: This would lose the implementation mapping and weaken future graph-grounded reasoning.

alternatives.option: Rewrite the original ADRs with code-level details
alternatives.rejected_because: This would change accepted ADR content instead of recording verified implementation evidence as a separate durable artifact.

expected: Future architectural queries can reference both the normative ADRs and the verified implementation surfaces
Graph-grounded reasoning about extension orchestration can cite concrete code anchors instead of restating ADR intent abstractly
Drift between ADR intent and implementation should be easier to detect during later inspections
risks: Implementation anchors may drift as files are refactored and will require refresh
This companion ADR is evidence-oriented and should not be mistaken for changing the original ADR decisions

guard_rails: Do NOT treat this record as modifying or superseding ADR-003 through ADR-007; it only captures verified implementation anchors.
Do NOT use numeric line numbers as canonical identity; prefer semantic anchors such as class and method names.
Do NOT claim enforcement beyond the verified surfaces without a fresh inspection.

decisions.title: Route GPT-5.5 Architect OpenAI calls through the Responses API

context.problem: The Architect extension added GPT-5.5 as an OpenAI model option, but its OpenAI non-streaming and tool-call paths still used Chat Completions even though GPT-5.5 guidance recommends the Responses API for reasoning, tool-calling, and multi-turn workloads.
constraints: Architect must preserve its existing provider abstraction and ArchitectResponse/ArchitectToolResponse contracts.
Architect tool-calling must continue to expose ToolUseRequest entries to the existing tool loop.
Existing OpenAI models that still use Chat Completions must not be regressed by the GPT-5.5 migration.
GPT-5.5 Responses API requests should use API-level reasoning effort and text verbosity controls with safe defaults.

decision.chosen: For OpenAI Architect calls whose model slug starts with gpt-5.5, route non-streaming and tool-call paths to /responses via a compatibility adapter. Leave existing Chat Completions paths in place for other OpenAI models and preserve the existing streaming implementation for now.

alternatives.option: Replace all OpenAI Architect calls with the Responses API immediately.
alternatives.rejected_because: This would risk regressions for existing OpenAI models and streaming behavior beyond the scope of the GPT-5.5 migration.

alternatives.option: Keep GPT-5.5 on Chat Completions because the existing abstraction already works for other OpenAI models.
alternatives.rejected_because: This conflicts with the GPT-5.5 migration guidance for reasoning, tool-calling, and multi-turn use cases.

expected: GPT-5.5 Architect non-streaming calls use /responses and can set reasoning.effort and text.verbosity.
GPT-5.5 Architect tool calls are adapted from Responses API function_call output items into the existing ToolUseRequest contract.
Existing non-GPT-5.5 OpenAI models continue using the prior Chat Completions implementation.
risks: The Responses API item schema may evolve or differ for hosted tools/phase metadata not yet represented in ArchitectToolResponse.
The current adapter is stateless and replays raw message/tool-result items rather than adopting previous_response_id state management.
GPT-5.5 streaming remains on the existing OpenAI streaming path until a separate streaming migration is implemented.

guard_rails: Do not route GPT-5.5 Architect reasoning/tool-call workloads back to Chat Completions without revisiting this ADR.
Do not remove the Chat Completions fallback for existing OpenAI models unless those models have been tested against the Responses API path.
Preserve the ArchitectToolResponse ToolUseRequest contract when changing Responses API parsing.

decisions.title: Use stateless Responses API for GPT-5.5 Architect initially

context.problem: The GPT-5.5 Responses API migration guide recommends stateful context mechanisms such as previous_response_id for multi-turn workflows, but Architect already uses DreamGraph as the authoritative memory/context source and the newly added GPT-5.5 adapter still needs correctness hardening for tool calls before introducing stateful optimization complexity.
constraints: DreamGraph remains the source of truth for memory and project context.
Architect GPT-5.5 tool-call correctness must be stable before optimizing state handling.
Avoid duplicating or diverging memory between OpenAI stored response state and DreamGraph graph/context assembly.
Initial GPT-5.5 implementation scope covers non-streaming and tool-call paths, not full provider migration.

decision.chosen: Keep the Architect GPT-5.5 Responses API adapter stateless initially. Continue replaying relevant context and tool-call items explicitly. Defer previous_response_id/store-based statefulness to a later optional optimization layer after GPT-5.5 tool-call correctness is verified.

alternatives.option: Adopt previous_response_id immediately for all GPT-5.5 Architect turns
alternatives.rejected_because: Adds state coordination complexity before tool-call correctness is stable and risks creating a second memory source outside DreamGraph.

alternatives.option: Use only Chat Completions until stateful Responses support is implemented
alternatives.rejected_because: Conflicts with the GPT-5.5 migration guidance for reasoning, tool-calling, and multi-turn workflows, and would block the already implemented Responses API adapter.

alternatives.option: Use OpenAI stored state as primary Architect memory
alternatives.rejected_because: Violates the architectural principle that DreamGraph is the source of memory and context.

expected: GPT-5.5 Architect calls remain easier to reason about and debug because each request carries explicit context and tool replay items.
DreamGraph continues to own long-term memory, graph context, decisions, workflows, and tensions.
Latency and token cost may be higher than a future stateful Responses implementation because context is replayed manually.
A later optimization can add previous_response_id/store once adapter correctness and observability are sufficient.
risks: Manual replay can increase prompt size and token cost for long conversations.
Some Responses API stateful optimizations and cached context benefits are deferred.
Future contributors may misinterpret absence of previous_response_id as an accidental migration gap unless this ADR is consulted.

guard_rails: Do not make OpenAI previous_response_id/store the primary Architect memory source; DreamGraph remains authoritative.
Do not add stateful Responses API handling for Architect until GPT-5.5 tool-call correctness has dedicated tests or equivalent verification.
If previous_response_id/store is added later, it must be treated as an optimization/cache layer and must not replace DreamGraph context retrieval or graph updates.
Keep stateless replay behavior available as a fallback even if stateful Responses support is introduced.

decisions.title: DreamGraph Explorer consistency and mutation safety model

context.problem: DreamGraph Explorer introduces a live graph view, SSE event stream, and curated mutation endpoints. Without explicit guard rails, future changes could weaken instance isolation, break optimistic concurrency, or create ambiguous client consistency semantics between snapshot state and live events.
constraints: Explorer serves both read-only graph browsing and curated mutation flows from the daemon HTTP surface.
Live updates are delivered via SSE with bounded replay and heartbeat semantics.
Mutation endpoints already require instance-scoped authorization, non-empty reason strings for governed intents, and optimistic concurrency via If-Match snapshot etags.
Explorer must remain safe for graph/cognitive state by funnelling writes through curated intents with audit coverage rather than arbitrary graph mutation.

decision.chosen: Adopt a consistency model where Explorer clients bootstrap from a versioned graph snapshot and then layer live SSE events on top with bounded best-effort replay. If replay gaps exceed the event buffer, clients must refetch the snapshot and reset local derived state. Adopt a mutation safety model where Explorer writes remain curated-intent only, require instance authentication on mutation routes, require If-Match etag checks for optimistic concurrency where configured, and append audit rows for both success and failure.

alternatives.option: Allow arbitrary direct Explorer graph writes without curated intents or audit
alternatives.rejected_because: This would bypass governance and make cognitive/graph state changes hard to reason about or trace.

alternatives.option: Use SSE as a fully durable source of truth with no required snapshot refetch on replay gaps
alternatives.rejected_because: The event stream is backed by a bounded ring buffer and cannot guarantee infinite resumability.

alternatives.option: Permit mutation endpoints without instance header or etag preconditions
alternatives.rejected_because: This would weaken instance isolation and increase the risk of stale-write races from outdated Explorer clients.

expected: Explorer clients have a clear contract: snapshot first, then live SSE, and reset on replay gaps.
Mutation flows stay auditable and bounded to approved intents.
Future Explorer changes can evolve UI and transport details without changing the core safety model.
Client implementations must handle gap/reset behavior and stale etag failures explicitly.
risks: SSE clients that ignore gap/reset semantics may show stale or divergent local state.
Strict If-Match preconditions can increase retry friction for highly dynamic views.
Legacy mode still allows mutation requests without UUID isolation, which reduces security guarantees in that mode.

guard_rails: Do NOT treat the Explorer SSE stream as a complete durable event log; clients must be able to refetch graph snapshot state after replay gaps.
Do NOT add arbitrary write endpoints under /explorer; Explorer mutations must remain curated intents routed through the mutation service with audit coverage.
Do NOT remove instance-header checks from Explorer mutation routes without replacing them with an equivalent or stronger isolation mechanism.
Do NOT remove If-Match optimistic concurrency from governed Explorer mutations without an explicit replacement concurrency strategy.
Do NOT allow governed Explorer mutations to proceed without recording reason/audit context when the mutation definition requires it.

decisions.title: DreamGraph Explorer unresolved operational tradeoffs

context.problem: DreamGraph Explorer has accepted safety guard rails, but several operational tradeoffs remain unresolved: legacy-mode authorization is weaker than strict instance isolation, bounded SSE replay creates replay-gap UX/reset costs, and optimistic concurrency via If-Match can create retry friction on high-churn views. These issues should be made explicit so future changes evaluate them deliberately rather than rediscovering them implicitly.
constraints: ADR-087 already establishes Explorer's binding consistency and mutation-safety model.
The current tension log does not contain explicit Explorer-specific unresolved tradeoff records.
Explorer must continue to support snapshot-first browsing, SSE live updates, and curated mutation flows.
Operational tradeoffs should be visible without weakening accepted guard rails.

decision.chosen: Record the unresolved Explorer operational tradeoffs as an explicit governance artifact so they remain visible: legacy-mode auth weakness vs deployment simplicity, bounded SSE replay vs lightweight transport, and strict If-Match concurrency vs user retry friction. Future Explorer changes should evaluate these tradeoffs against ADR-087 guard rails instead of relaxing the guard rails silently.

alternatives.option: Leave the tradeoffs implicit in code and ADR risk text only
alternatives.rejected_because: Important unresolved concerns would be harder to discover and easier to regress during later feature work.

alternatives.option: Relax the existing Explorer guard rails now to reduce friction
alternatives.rejected_because: That would trade away safety and consistency without a dedicated replacement design.

alternatives.option: Wait for production incidents before documenting these tradeoffs
alternatives.rejected_because: Reactive documentation would lose architectural context and delay mitigation planning.

expected: Explorer governance now distinguishes binding guard rails from unresolved operating tensions.
Future work can explicitly target legacy auth hardening, replay-gap UX, and stale-etag ergonomics.
Teams reviewing Explorer changes have a stable reference for known tradeoffs.
risks: This ADR records tensions but does not itself resolve them.
Some users may interpret the documented tradeoffs as defects even when they are accepted temporary compromises.
Additional follow-up tracking may still be needed if operational evidence grows.

guard_rails: Do NOT remove or weaken ADR-087 guard rails when addressing Explorer operational tradeoffs; tradeoff mitigation must preserve snapshot-first consistency and curated mutation safety.
Do NOT treat legacy-mode authorization, replay-gap resets, or stale-etag retries as solved without explicit replacement design and validation.
Do NOT optimize Explorer UX by bypassing audit, instance isolation, or optimistic concurrency requirements without a superseding ADR.

decisions.title: Lazy-Created JSON-Backed Resources Bootstrap Empty and Degrade Gracefully on ENOENT

context.problem: Some registered DreamGraph resources are backed by JSON files that may not exist yet during bootstrap or in intentionally inert configurations. Clients should see stable resource semantics instead of bootstrap-state failures such as ENOENT or INVALID_URI when the resource is known but its backing file has not been created yet.
constraints: Registered resource URIs must remain stable regardless of whether their backing JSON file has been created yet.
Instance data storage is authoritative for ADRs and resource backing state; workspace files are not the ADR source of truth.
The datastore bootstrap path is intentionally inert when no DATABASE_URL is configured, but the resource surface should still be queryable.
Client-facing query semantics should hide expected bootstrap absence while still preserving explicit invalid-resource errors for unknown URIs.
The solution should align tool behavior and bootstrap behavior so file-on-disk truth converges with resource-registration truth.

decision.chosen: Adopt a two-part policy for lazy-created JSON-backed resources: (1) bootstrap creates known backing files in an empty canonical state where appropriate, such as datastores.json initialized to []; and (2) resource-query tooling treats ENOENT for known registered JSON-backed resources as an empty resource instead of surfacing an internal error. Unknown resource URIs must still return INVALID_URI.

alternatives.option: Surface ENOENT to clients for missing backing files
alternatives.rejected_because: This leaks expected bootstrap state into the client contract and makes a registered resource appear broken during inert or first-run states.

alternatives.option: Bootstrap empty files only, with no tool-level ENOENT degradation
alternatives.rejected_because: This leaves clients exposed to runtime failures when older instances or partial deployments lack the expected seed file.

alternatives.option: Tool-level graceful degradation only, without creating empty files during bootstrap
alternatives.rejected_because: This keeps behavior stable for clients but allows file-on-disk truth to diverge from resource-registration truth longer than necessary.

expected: Known JSON-backed resources can be queried safely before any substantive configuration exists.
The no-database-configured case returns an empty datastore list instead of an internal error.
Bootstrap semantics become more predictable because known empty resources have canonical on-disk representations.
Operational debugging remains clear because unknown URIs still fail explicitly with INVALID_URI.
risks: Graceful ENOENT degradation may hide some genuine deployment mistakes for known resources if operators expect the file to exist already.
Creating empty backing files during bootstrap introduces small amounts of inert instance data for users who never configure those resources.

guard_rails: Do NOT return INTERNAL_ERROR for ENOENT when querying a known registered JSON-backed resource that is allowed to start empty; return the canonical empty shape instead.
Do NOT treat unknown resource URIs as empty resources; they must continue to fail explicitly as INVALID_URI.
Do NOT rely on workspace ADR files as the source of truth for this decision; the daemon instance ADR store is authoritative.
Do NOT remove bootstrap creation of canonical empty backing files for lazy-created resources without revisiting this ADR.

decisions.title: Cold-start mode dual exit (entity-count OR cycle/time window)

context.problem: Normalizer's strict promotion thresholds (confidence ≥ 0.62, evidence ≥ 0.4, evidence_count ≥ 2, entity-existence required) are unreachable on a cold-start graph because the evidence signal is circular — entities must already be in the graph to count. validated_edges.json stays empty and the dream→normalize→promote loop never produces actionable output on fresh instances.
constraints: Must terminate (no infinite cold-start)
Must not be defeated by very small or domain-narrow repos that legitimately contain few entities
Must not prematurely tighten on slow-growing graphs
Tuning floors must be empirically observable, not guessed

decision.chosen: Add a cold-start mode in the normalizer with relaxed thresholds (drop entity-existence requirement, count domain/keyword overlap as evidence, lower confidence floor to ~0.50). Mode exits via a DUAL condition — whichever fires first: (A) entity-count threshold (≥ 50 entities AND ≥ 10 validated edges), OR (B) bootstrap window elapsed (20 dream cycles OR 24h of daemon uptime). Telemetry records exit_reason: "size" | "window" | "manual".

alternatives.option: Entity-count threshold only
alternatives.rejected_because: Tiny / domain-narrow repos may never reach the count and stay in cold-start forever.

alternatives.option: Time/cycle window only
alternatives.rejected_because: Slow-growing graphs would prematurely tighten before enough evidence accumulated.

alternatives.option: Lower thresholds permanently
alternatives.rejected_because: Sacrifices long-term graph quality for short-term bootstrap convenience.

expected: Fresh instances begin producing validated edges within the first ~20 cycles
Telemetry on exit_reason allows empirical tuning of the 50/10/20/24h floors
Existing mature instances behave identically once they exit the bootstrap window
risks: Relaxed thresholds may admit lower-quality edges during bootstrap window
Dual-condition logic adds branching to a hot path in the normalizer
exit_reason telemetry must actually be reviewed for the tuning loop to close

guard_rails: Do NOT remove the dual-condition exit — entity-count and window must both remain
Do NOT raise the relaxed floor above 0.50 confidence without revisiting this ADR
Do NOT extend the bootstrap window beyond 24h without telemetry justification
exit_reason field MUST remain populated on every cold-start exit event

decisions.title: Hard-reserved token slice for graph evidence in architect context

context.problem: The context builder treats graph evidence (features, workflows, tensions, ADRs) as optional — gated by intentConfidence ≥ 0.5 and a literal source_files substring match. Under token pressure, graph evidence is the first thing trimmed. The architect ends up file-centric in practice despite a graph-first design intent.
constraints: Must work across 8k → 128k+ context windows
Must not drown core logic in very large windows
Curated content only, no raw dumps
Confidence markers must be preserved so the LLM can weight validated vs candidate evidence

decision.chosen: Reserve a hard token slice: 70% core logic / 15% user request + active code/selection / 15% graph evidence. Absolute caps per window: 8k → 800–1200 tokens; 32k → 2k–4k tokens; 128k+ → dynamic, capped at ~10% of window. Graph slice is curated only — selected node + immediate neighborhood, transitive impacted nodes (depth ≤ 2, ranked), tensions touching the request, ADR constraints touching the request, plus confidence markers. Golden rule: better 300 curated tokens than 3000 garbage tokens.

alternatives.option: Keep graph evidence opt-in by intent confidence
alternatives.rejected_because: Token-pressure trimming consistently strips it first; defeats the graph-first design.

alternatives.option: Always inject full graph as raw JSON
alternatives.rejected_because: Drowns the model, blows the budget, and produces worse answers than no graph at all.

alternatives.option: Percentage-only with no absolute caps
alternatives.rejected_because: 128k+ windows would dedicate 19k+ tokens to graph evidence and dilute core logic.

expected: Architect always has at least some graph grounding regardless of intent confidence
Context builder must rank-and-trim instead of concatenate-and-hope
LLM can naturally weight validated edges over candidate ones via confidence markers
Predictable token budgets make response latency more stable
risks: Hard reservation reduces room for raw code in tight windows
Ranking algorithm becomes a quality bottleneck — bad ranking = bad answers
Curation logic adds CPU cost on every architect invocation

guard_rails: Do NOT remove the 15% graph slice without revisiting this ADR
Do NOT exceed the absolute caps on small windows (8k/32k) — quality over quantity
Do NOT inject raw graph dumps into the slice — curation is mandatory
Confidence markers MUST stay attached to every graph evidence item

decisions.title: LLM-readiness watcher with fingerprinted re-runs for graph bootstrap

context.problem: dg init may or may not arrive with a working LLM. Default lmstudio/ollama templates have populated env vars but are useless until the user starts the local server and loads a model. Personal templates with API keys may be ready immediately. No current trigger fires the bootstrap chain (scan_project + enrich_seed_data + ADR discovery + first dream cycle) the moment the LLM actually becomes usable, so instances stay on templates/default schema stubs indefinitely.
constraints: Readiness must reflect actual LLM availability, not env-var presence
Bootstrap must run exactly once per (provider, model, endpoint) configuration
Provider switches must not waste a full source re-scan
Users need a manual escape hatch
Source-file changes after bootstrap need an incremental delta path

decision.chosen: Add an LLM-readiness watcher in the daemon that fires the bootstrap chain the first time a real completion call against the configured provider returns successfully. Re-run policy: fingerprint = hash(provider + model + url); bootstrap chain runs once per fingerprint. Fingerprint changes trigger re-enrichment ONLY (not a re-scan), reusing existing entity ids and refreshing description/domain/keywords/links. Surface progress via cognitive_status. Add a `dg bootstrap` CLI verb for manual retrigger. Add a debounced file-watcher delta scan for incremental updates after first bootstrap.

alternatives.option: Auto-scan during dg init
alternatives.rejected_because: LLM config isn't ready at init time for local-LLM templates; would require redoing the scan after enrichment.

alternatives.option: Poll env-var presence to detect readiness
alternatives.rejected_because: False positives on local-LLM templates whose env vars are populated long before the model is loaded.

alternatives.option: Re-scan on every fingerprint change
alternatives.rejected_because: Wasteful — source files haven't moved; only semantic metadata depends on the model.

expected: Instances bootstrap automatically the moment a real LLM is reachable, regardless of when that happens
Provider switches are cheap (re-enrichment only) but still refresh model-dependent metadata
dg bootstrap CLI verb makes the watcher debuggable and gives users an escape hatch
Delta scans keep the graph fresh without a full re-scan on every file save
risks: Real completion call costs tokens / startup latency
Fingerprint hash collisions are theoretically possible (mitigated by including url)
Debounced file-watcher needs careful tuning to avoid scan storms

guard_rails: Readiness check MUST be a real completion call, not env-var presence
Fingerprint changes MUST NOT trigger a full source re-scan
Existing entity ids MUST be preserved across re-enrichment
dg bootstrap CLI verb MUST remain available as a manual override

decisions.title: Progressive ADR enforcement (advisory → soft → strict)

context.problem: ADRs are currently paper. discoverAndRecordADRs() is never invoked, the normalizer has no ADR guard rails, and the architect only consults ADRs when the user prompt matches a regex. Code changes can silently violate accepted ADRs. Hard-blocking by default would create user resentment and obstruct legitimate exception cases.
constraints: Humans must always retain manual override capability
Default behavior must build trust, not friction
Teams with stricter policy needs must have an opt-in escalation path
Enforcement level must be configurable per instance

decision.chosen: Three progressive levels controlled by DREAMGRAPH_ADR_ENFORCEMENT=advisory|soft|strict (default: advisory). Advisory: log warning, create tension signal, explain violation risk in architect response — no blocking. Soft (workspace opt-in): architect surfaces a confirmation prompt before proceeding ("This conflicts with ADR-004. Proceed anyway? [yes/no]"). Strict (team setting): blocks AUTONOMOUS promotion only — normalizer refuses to promote ADR-violating edges and architect refuses to apply ADR-violating patches without an explicit manual override gesture. Humans may always override manually at every level.

alternatives.option: Hard-block by default
alternatives.rejected_because: Generates friction faster than it generates value; obstructs legitimate exception cases.

alternatives.option: Pure advisory only (no strict path)
alternatives.rejected_because: Insufficient for teams with formal architecture compliance requirements.

alternatives.option: Per-ADR enforcement level
alternatives.rejected_because: Configuration sprawl; project-wide policy is the right granularity for this version.

expected: ADRs become enforceable instead of decorative
Default advisory mode builds user trust by explaining rather than blocking
Soft mode adds friction only proportional to risk
Strict mode satisfies team policy without locking out human judgment
Per-instance config keeps the choice local to project risk tolerance
risks: Soft-mode confirmation prompts may be ignored / clicked through habitually
Strict mode could surprise users who didn't realize an ADR was in effect
Tension signals from advisory mode could create alert fatigue

guard_rails: Manual human override MUST work at every enforcement level
Default level MUST remain advisory — never escalate by default
Strict mode MUST only block autonomous promotion, never block humans
DREAMGRAPH_ADR_ENFORCEMENT env var name MUST NOT change without migration notes

decisions.title: export_living_docs covers datastores, auxiliary entities, and tensions

context.problem: After Slice 4B (tension resolution lifecycle) and Slice 5B (extended scanning of datastores + auxiliary entities: MCP tools, test suites, configuration files, automation scripts), the living-docs exporter only emitted features, data_model, workflows, architecture, ui_registry, cognitive_status, and api_reference. New canonical knowledge stores (`datastores.json`, `auxiliary_entities.json`, `tension_log.json` with resolution candidates) had no published surface, breaking the documentation-sync rule and hiding live cognitive state from consumers.
constraints: Must be backward compatible — existing section names and `all` semantics keep working.
Must not require LLM calls — generators are pure JSON-to-Markdown transformations.
Must gracefully degrade when source JSON is missing or empty (no error, just zero buffers).
Must respect existing format adapters (docusaurus / nextra / mkdocs / plain) via `frontmatter` helper.
Must keep `cognitive_status` opt-in via `include_cognitive` even under `all`.

decision.chosen: Extend the `LivingDocsSection` union with `datastores`, `auxiliary`, and `tensions`, add corresponding loaders (`loadDatastores`, `loadAuxiliaryEntitiesFile`) and pure generators (`genDatastores`, `genAuxiliary`, `genTensions`), and wire them into VALID_SECTIONS, the `all` expansion, the dispatch ladder, and the index `sectionLabels`. The auxiliary section groups by `kind` (mcp_tool, test_suite, configuration, automation_script). The tensions section surfaces open-by-type counts, top-25 by urgency, and the Slice 4B resolution candidates with strategy + validation window.

alternatives.option: Emit datastores/auxiliary/tensions only via new dedicated tools
alternatives.rejected_because: Would fragment the docs surface, force consumers to discover and stitch together separate exporters, and duplicate format adapter logic.

alternatives.option: Roll datastores into the existing `data_model` section
alternatives.rejected_because: Datastores have a distinct schema (kind/url_hint/tables[] introspected by `scan_database`) that is operationally different from logical data_model entries, and bundling them would obscure the introspection vs. modeling distinction.

alternatives.option: Skip tensions in living docs because state is volatile
alternatives.rejected_because: Resolution candidates from Slice 4B are an architecturally significant surface and consumers need to see the heuristic strategies in published docs.

expected: Living docs reflects the full v8.2 entity surface — Slice 4B + 5B work is discoverable.
Documentation-sync rule (.github/copilot-instructions.md) is honored for the new stores.
Auxiliary entity coverage gives future tooling a stable per-kind URL pattern.
risks: Tension snapshots are volatile — exported tensions page can drift between exports; consumers must understand it is a snapshot, not a log.
Auxiliary kind taxonomy is fixed in `KIND_ORDER`; introducing a fifth kind requires touching the generator.
Datastore pages depend on `scan_database` having populated `tables[]`; exports will be sparse until the daemon has introspected each datastore.

guard_rails: Do NOT remove or rename the `datastores`, `auxiliary`, or `tensions` section identifiers — they are part of the public tool contract.
Do NOT make any of the new generators depend on LLM calls or network IO; they must remain pure JSON-to-Markdown.
Do NOT include `cognitive_status` in the `all` expansion implicitly; the `include_cognitive` opt-in must continue to gate it.
Do NOT silently swallow load errors without returning an empty buffer set — failure to read should not crash the whole export.

Any new entity store added in the future MUST also extend the exporter (LivingDocsSection union, loader, generator, sectionLabels, VALID_SECTIONS, all-expansion, dispatch) before being considered shipped.

decisions.title: Anchor cognitive timeline analysis on real ISO timestamps via cycleFromIso

context.problem: Cognitive timeline analytics in causal.ts and temporal.ts (causal lag, urgency-over-time trajectories, first/last-observed timestamps) were derived from synthetic counters (currentCycle - ttl, original.occurrences) instead of the real ISO timestamps already carried by dream-history entries and tension events. Active tensions all collapsed onto currentCycle and resolved tensions onto original.occurrences, so trajectory pattern=spike was unreachable, CausalLink.first_observed/last_observed were synthetic, and lag arithmetic was meaningless.
constraints: No schema change to existing data files (dream_history.json, tension_log.json must remain readable)
No new runtime dependency
Lookup must be O(log n) on long histories
engine.loadDreamHistory()/loadTensions() must remain the data source

decision.chosen: Add a buildHistoryIndex() + cycleFromIso() helper pair in both cognitive/causal.ts and cognitive/temporal.ts. Both consume engine.loadDreamHistory(), build a sorted {ts, cycle}[] index from per-cycle generated_at, and binary-search for the largest ts <= target ISO. All trajectory anchors and CausalLink.first_observed/last_observed derive from real ISO via this pair. The currentCycle - ttl and original.occurrences heuristics are removed. Rejected alternatives: extracting a shared helper now (broadens scope), persisting resolution_cycle on ResolvedTension at write time (schema migration), recomputing cycle from a synthetic monotonic counter (the bug being removed).

expected: Trajectory pattern=spike becomes structurally reachable for tensions whose urgency actually spiked between cycles
CausalLink.first_observed/last_observed carry meaningful ISO strings derived from real cause/effect events
Lag values in propagation_hotspots reflect real cycle deltas and become safe to act on
Resolved-tension resolution_cycle reflects the actual resolution moment instead of original.occurrences
risks: Two ~30 LOC helpers (one per module) drift out of sync until extraction
Building the index per call has measurable cost on very large histories (mitigated by the 5s mtime cache on loadJsonData)
Non-UTC ISO offsets could sort incorrectly (mitigated: all writers use new Date().toISOString() which is always UTC Z)
detectSeasonalPatterns() had to be stubbed pending a DreamHistoryEntry schema change to record per-cycle per-domain tension counts

guard_rails: If a third consumer of cycleFromIso appears, hoist buildHistoryIndex/cycleFromIso to a shared module before adding a third copy
Keep the fallback to `now` when first_seen/resolved_at is missing or unparseable — older logs may lack the field
Do NOT replace cycleFromIso with currentCycle-based heuristics; that regressed the analytics once already
Do NOT remove the NOTE block on detectSeasonalPatterns without first extending DreamHistoryEntry to carry per-cycle per-domain tension counts

decisions.title: Discipline manifest must mirror the live MCP tool registry 1:1

context.problem: src/discipline/manifest.ts had a 56-tool TOOL_CLASSIFICATIONS map but the server registered 72 tools. 17 live MCP tools (including init_graph, scan_project, edit_file, lucid_dream, graph_rag_retrieve, get_cognitive_preamble, and discipline_record_tool_call) had no classification. tool-proxy.checkToolPermission and the discipline manifest exposed to clients were silently incomplete. The header doc-comment claimed '53 MCP tools', further understating coverage.
constraints: Phase permissions for new tools must be chosen by analogy with the closest existing peer (e.g. all *_file tools mirror create_file's posture; lucid_* mirror dream_cycle's internal-only posture)
Cognitive tools that run only inside the engine lifecycle must have allowed_phases=[]
Tools that mutate persistent target files must carry target-write semantics + ['execute'] phase + plan_entry=true
The doc-comment count and the actual TOOL_CLASSIFICATIONS map size must agree

decision.chosen: Treat src/discipline/manifest.ts as a strict mirror of the live MCP tool registry. Every server.tool('name', ...) registration must have a matching TOOL_CLASSIFICATIONS entry, and the doc-comment header must report the same count. Reconciled this pass by adding 17 missing classifications (truth/analysis/write/file_operation/cognitive/verification categories) and updating '53 MCP tools' to '73 MCP tools (72 server + 1 local extension equivalent)'. The single non-server entry (read_local_file) is the VS Code extension's filesystem peer of read_source_code and is referenced by MANDATORY_TOOL_RULES. A diff check (Select-String 'server\\.tool\\(' vs Select-String 'tool_name:') must report 0 missing and 0 extras.

expected: tool-proxy.checkToolPermission() now sees ground truth for every registered tool; phase gating is no longer silently bypassed for unclassified tools
buildManifest() exported to clients reflects every real capability
Discipline session enforcement covers the full surface area, not just the legacy 56 tools
Future contributors get a CI-style diff signal when they add a tool without classifying it
risks: Future tool additions can re-introduce drift if contributors do not also update manifest.ts
Phase permissions chosen by analogy may be wrong for a genuinely novel tool category
The extension's read_local_file entry creates a single 'classified but not server-registered' exception that future maintainers must understand

guard_rails: Do NOT add a new server.tool registration without simultaneously adding a TOOL_CLASSIFICATIONS entry and updating the header count
Do NOT classify a tool by guessing posture — mirror the nearest existing peer's category, target, allowed_phases, audit_trail, and plan_entry
Do NOT remove the 'read_local_file' entry without first removing the corresponding extension capability from extensions/vscode/src/local-tools.ts
Always run the registered-vs-classified diff (Select-String) before merging discipline changes

decisions.title: All persistent JSON writes use atomicWriteFile (temp + fdatasync + rename)

context.problem: Several CLI commands (attach, export, fork) and the engine-env initializer wrote persistent JSON state with raw writeFile/writeFileSync. A crash or power loss mid-write would leave a truncated or zero-byte file in place of the previous valid state, with no recovery path.
constraints: No introduction of native fs-extra or graceful-fs deps — use built-in fs/promises and fs only
Sync writes (engine-env init) must also be atomic — mid-init crash must not leave a corrupt instance.json
atomicWriteFile must default to UTF-8 so callers do not have to repeat the encoding flag
Failure path must clean up the orphan .tmp where possible without masking the original error

decision.chosen: All persistent JSON state writes go through src/utils/atomic-write.ts (open \u2192 writeFile \u2192 fdatasync \u2192 close \u2192 rename) for the async path. The synchronous engine-env initializer in src/utils/engine-env.ts mirrors the same pattern with openSync \u2192 writeFileSync \u2192 fdatasyncSync \u2192 closeSync \u2192 renameSync, and unlinks the orphan .tmp on failure. Audit pass converted 8 sites: attach.ts (3), export.ts (3), fork.ts (1), engine-env.ts (1).

expected: Crash or power loss during a write leaves the original file intact and at most a harmless orphan .tmp
Operators can trust that data/*.json files are either the prior valid version or the new valid version, never a partial truncation
New code adding a writeFile against persistent state is an obvious code-smell visible in review
risks: Inline sync atomic pattern in engine-env.ts duplicates the helper's logic and can drift
The orphan .tmp cleanup is best-effort; if both rename and unlink fail, the .tmp lingers (harmless but noisy)
Atomic rename is per-filesystem; cross-device renames will fail (mitigated: temp file is in same directory as target)

guard_rails: Do NOT add a raw writeFile() / writeFileSync() against any data/*.json or instance.json path — always go through atomicWriteFile or its sync mirror
Do NOT skip fdatasync; rename without fdatasync can still expose torn writes on some filesystems
Do NOT swallow rename errors silently — propagate so the caller knows the write was not durable
When adding new sync write sites, replicate the engine-env.ts inline pattern rather than blocking on the async helper

decisions.title: Adaptive Result Delivery Uses Targets, Expectations, and Explicit Compromise Instead of Hard Limits

context.problem: DreamGraph tool and transport responses can vary in size and fidelity across producer, serialization, transport, client, and history layers. Modeling these behaviors as fixed hard result limits leads to incorrect reasoning, misleading diagnostics, and brittle implementation choices. For this kind of cognitive system, hard-size enforcement is a poor fit because it hides partial success and prevents adaptive recovery strategies.
constraints: The system operates across multiple layers where payload degradation may occur after successful tool execution.
Response sizing behavior is soft and context-dependent rather than governed by a single authoritative constant.
The system must support progressive narrowing and recovery when large responses are difficult to deliver intact.
Existing tooling and callers may need backward-compatible response evolution rather than abrupt clipping or hard failure semantics.

decision.chosen: DreamGraph will not model response delivery through fixed hard result limits as the primary policy. Instead, it will use adaptive targets and expectations for result delivery, and when ideal delivery cannot be preserved it should favor explicit compromise signaling and recovery guidance over hard-cap language or premature clipping.

alternatives.option: Keep or introduce fixed hard result limits
alternatives.rejected_because: This creates false certainty, encourages brittle behavior, conflates producer success with downstream delivery loss, and is a poor fit for adaptive cognitive tooling.

alternatives.option: Silently clip oversized results without signaling
alternatives.rejected_because: This destroys context, obscures failure modes, and prevents callers from recovering intelligently.

alternatives.option: Treat truncation as purely a client concern with no architectural guidance
alternatives.rejected_because: This leaves the system without a shared reasoning model and leads to inconsistent diagnostics and response-shaping decisions.

expected: Diagnostics will shift from hard-cap language toward target/expectation/compromise language.
Tool and transport behavior can evolve adaptively without violating an artificial constant-limit model.
Large-response handling should increasingly provide recovery hints and navigable structure rather than relying on clipping.
Agents and humans will be better able to distinguish producer success from downstream compromise.
risks: Without careful wording, adaptive behavior may become too vague for implementers.
Different subsystems may interpret targets and compromises inconsistently.
Some callers may still assume hard ceilings and require migration in language or expectations.

guard_rails: Do not describe result delivery as governed by a single hard constant unless code and runtime policy explicitly prove that is true.
Prefer additive response metadata and explicit compromise signaling over silent clipping.
When large payload delivery degrades, preserve or expose recovery paths such as narrowing, sub-entity targeting, or structured summaries.
Distinguish tool execution success from downstream delivery fidelity in diagnostics and user-facing reasoning.

decisions.title: Canonical M1 runtime metrics snapshot aligns /metrics, system://metrics, and query_runtime_metrics

context.problem: Runtime observability surfaces were diverging: internal metrics sources existed, but the canonical contract for M1 runtime observability was not uniformly represented across the shared adapter, HTTP endpoint, resource surface, and tool surface. Without a single snapshot schema, future consumers could drift and produce incompatible metrics payloads.
constraints: Preserve graceful behavior when runtime metrics are disabled or no external endpoint is configured.
Use the existing shared consolidation point in src/observability/runtime-metrics.ts rather than creating parallel metrics adapters.
Keep the initial M1 schema operationally useful even if some buckets are derived heuristically from current tool and graph metrics sources.
Allow local/private HTTP exposure for /metrics in M1 without requiring public deployment hardening.
Align resource and tool surfaces to the same canonical snapshot semantics wherever feasible.
