decision.chosen: Adopt src/observability/runtime-metrics.ts as the canonical producer of RuntimeMetricsSnapshotV1 using the nested M1 schema. The HTTP /metrics endpoint, the system://metrics resource, and the query_runtime_metrics tool should all align to this canonical snapshot model. In M1, /metrics is gated by an explicit enable flag and restricted to local/private use, while resource/tool surfaces may use the same snapshot directly or via configured endpoint retrieval depending on context.

alternatives.option: Let each surface (/metrics, resources, tools) shape its own metrics payload independently
alternatives.rejected_because: This would reintroduce contract drift and make observability consumers unreliable.

alternatives.option: Keep the previous flat metrics schema until all downstream consumers are implemented
alternatives.rejected_because: The flat schema does not match the approved M1 plan and would force later breaking changes across more consumers.

alternatives.option: Expose only an external endpoint-backed query_runtime_metrics tool and avoid internal canonicalization
alternatives.rejected_because: This would make local validation harder and leave resource/HTTP surfaces semantically inconsistent.

expected: Runtime observability consumers have a single M1 snapshot contract to target.
Future additions to metrics buckets can be made in one shared adapter and flow to HTTP/resource/tool surfaces consistently.
There is a clear implementation anchor for M1 observability alignment across runtime surfaces.
risks: Some current bucket derivations are heuristic because existing low-level metrics sources were not originally designed around the exact M1 schema.
Consumers not yet migrated may still assume the previous flat shape.
Async/sync signature changes in the canonical snapshot producer may require follow-up alignment if hidden call sites exist.

guard_rails: Do NOT introduce a second canonical runtime metrics adapter while RuntimeMetricsSnapshotV1 is owned by src/observability/runtime-metrics.ts.
Do NOT let /metrics, system://metrics, or query_runtime_metrics drift to incompatible payload schemas without explicitly revisiting this decision.
Do NOT expose /metrics broadly by default in M1; keep it explicitly enabled and locally constrained unless a later decision hardens it for wider deployment.
Do NOT treat absent or partial runtime data as evidence of feature health; observability gaps remain possible.

decisions.title: SDK webhooks are core service first and plugin-consumable later

context.problem: The SDK roadmap needed to decide whether webhooks should be implemented as plugin-provided functionality or as a core DreamGraph service before plugins consume webhook capabilities.
constraints: Webhook delivery touches secrets, signing, retries, dead-letter queues, replay, and operator trust.
Plugin code must not receive broad authority over delivery security or operational reliability by default.
The plugin SDK should expose stable consumable capabilities only after the core service defines the trust and operational model.
related_tensions: core platform responsibility vs plugin flexibility

decision.chosen: Implement webhook delivery as a core service first. Make it plugin-consumable later through host-mediated capabilities once delivery, signing, retry, DLQ, replay, and audit semantics are mature.

alternatives.option: Let plugins implement webhook delivery directly in MVP
alternatives.rejected_because: Would delegate secrets, signing, retries, replay, and failure handling to arbitrary plugins before the trust model is established.

alternatives.option: Exclude webhooks entirely from the plugin roadmap
alternatives.rejected_because: Plugins are expected to benefit from webhook events later, but they should consume a core service rather than own delivery.

expected: Core owns webhook security and delivery semantics.
Plugins can later subscribe to or emit webhook-relevant events through a constrained host-mediated API.
The MVP plugin surface remains smaller and safer.
risks: Core webhook implementation may become a bottleneck for plugin-driven integrations.
The later plugin-consumable API must avoid leaking secrets or replay authority.

guard_rails: Do not grant plugins arbitrary webhook delivery authority before the core webhook service exists.
Do not store signing secrets or retry/DLQ policy inside untrusted plugin packages.
Do not expose webhook replay or delivery mutation operations to plugins without explicit host-mediated authorization.

decisions.title: Plugin management is bundled into the existing dg CLI

context.problem: The SDK roadmap needed to decide whether plugin management should use a separate toolchain or become part of the existing DreamGraph command-line interface.
constraints: Plugin management is instance administration.
Operators should not need a separate plugin-specific CLI toolchain for normal administration.
The existing dg CLI is the natural administrative surface for DreamGraph instances.
related_tensions: single administrative surface vs separate plugin toolchain

decision.chosen: Bundle plugin management commands into the existing dg CLI under dg plugin rather than creating a separate CLI.

alternatives.option: Create a standalone plugin CLI
alternatives.rejected_because: Would split instance administration across multiple tools and increase operator burden.

alternatives.option: Leave plugin management entirely manual
alternatives.rejected_because: Would undermine repeatable installation, inspection, enabling, disabling, and lifecycle management.

expected: Operators administer plugins through the same dg tool used for the rest of DreamGraph.
Documentation and automation can standardize on dg plugin commands.
Future plugin lifecycle commands should fit under the existing CLI command hierarchy.
risks: The dg CLI can become crowded if plugin commands are not organized carefully.
CLI implementation must preserve clear separation between plugin administration and runtime plugin authority.

guard_rails: Do not introduce a separate first-party plugin management CLI without superseding this decision.
Keep plugin lifecycle administration under dg plugin or a clearly compatible dg subcommand hierarchy.
Do not let CLI convenience bypass plugin trust, signing, allowlist, or capability checks.

decisions.title: Provider adapters use a hybrid trust model with core presets and signed or allowlisted plugins

context.problem: The SDK roadmap needed to decide how to support provider-specific integrations such as Gemini, OAuth bridges, CLI bridges, and OpenRouter-like providers without contaminating architect-llm or granting unsafe authority to arbitrary plugins.
constraints: architect-llm should remain lean and protocol-pure, consuming normalized LLM/MCP surfaces rather than provider-specific quirks.
Provider adapters may require network access, process execution, OAuth/device-code flows, secrets, retries, and provider-specific error normalization.
Safe/simple OpenAI-compatible providers can often be represented as core presets without a full plugin adapter.
Risky adapters must not receive arbitrary network or process authority by default.

decision.chosen: Use a hybrid provider-adapter model: implement safe/simple providers as core presets; allow risky or complex adapters through signed or allowlisted plugins; never grant arbitrary network or process authority by default. Adapters normalize provider quirks behind a stable LLM/MCP-facing surface so architect-llm stays protocol-pure.

alternatives.option: Put Gemini and other provider-specific behavior directly into architect-llm
alternatives.rejected_because: Would contaminate the architectural reasoning layer with provider-specific request shaping, safety settings, streaming formats, tool-call conversion, auth, and error handling.

alternatives.option: Allow any plugin to perform arbitrary network or process calls as a provider adapter
alternatives.rejected_because: Would violate the SDK trust model and expose secrets, operator environment, and process/network authority too broadly.

alternatives.option: Only support core provider presets and never plugin adapters
alternatives.rejected_because: Would keep the core safer but limit integration with complex providers whose quirks are better isolated in optional adapters.

expected: architect-llm can remain focused on normalized protocol semantics.
Gemini-style integrations can live in adapters that handle provider-specific content parts, tool calls, safety blocks, streaming chunks, model IDs, auth, and errors.
OpenRouter and other OpenAI-compatible providers can start as core presets where possible.
Security review can focus on signed or allowlisted adapters for providers requiring elevated authority.
risks: The normalized provider contract may be hard to design across Gemini, OpenAI-compatible providers, OAuth-backed services, and CLI bridges.
Adapter signing and allowlisting infrastructure must be implemented before broad third-party provider adapters are safe.
Core presets may accumulate too many special cases if not kept strict.

guard_rails: Do not add provider-specific Gemini-style quirks directly to architect-llm without superseding this decision.
Do not grant provider-adapter plugins arbitrary fetch, socket, shell, or child_process authority by default.
Require signed or explicitly allowlisted status for risky provider adapters that need network, process, OAuth, or secret-bearing capabilities.
Keep simple OpenAI-compatible providers as core presets when they do not require new trust boundaries.
Provider adapters must present normalized LLM/MCP-facing requests, responses, tool-call events, stream events, errors, and capability metadata to core consumers.

decisions.title: SDK host loader discovers declared ESM plugins only from instance roots and keeps runtime loading out of M1

context.problem: The SDK roadmap needs a stable host loading model before plugin APIs become public. Without an explicit discovery and module-loading rule, plugin authors and daemon code could depend on accidental paths, CJS/ESM behavior, or early runtime loading semantics that are hard to revoke.
constraints: M1 must ship SDK and host package skeletons without runtime plugin loading.
DreamGraph is a type=module Node project, so ESM should be the default module format.
Plugin discovery must be instance-admin controlled, not implicit global scanning.
Version skew must be handled through manifest engine.dreamgraph ranges before any plugin code executes.
In-process execution is trusted-only until later worker isolation hardening.
related_tensions: SDK packaging must be stable before plugin runtime loading exists

decision.chosen: Use an explicit host loading model: discover plugins only from <instance>/plugins/*/plugin.json and packages listed in instance.json plugins; target ESM modules as the supported plugin format; validate plugin.json and engine.dreamgraph before importing plugin code; keep @dreamgraph/host in M1 as a schema/contract package with no runtime plugin execution; defer in-process loading to the trusted M3 model behind the host safety switch.

alternatives.option: Scan all node_modules packages matching dreamgraph-plugin-* automatically
alternatives.rejected_because: Implicit scanning expands trust and supply-chain risk and conflicts with instance-admin control.

alternatives.option: Support CJS and ESM equally from day one
alternatives.rejected_because: Dual loader semantics create packaging ambiguity before the SDK surface is stable.

alternatives.option: Implement runtime plugin loading in M1
alternatives.rejected_because: M1 is intentionally a skeleton/schema phase; loading before capability gates and audit artifacts are stable would freeze unsafe contracts.

expected: Plugin installation remains explicit and auditable.
M1 can validate package shape and manifests without executing third-party code.
Future M3 loader work has a clear discovery and validation sequence.
ESM-first package design avoids dual-package hazards in the initial SDK.
risks: Some plugin authors may expect automatic npm package discovery.
CJS-only plugin authors will need migration guidance or a later compatibility decision.
Host package may appear underpowered until M3 because it intentionally does not load plugins.

guard_rails: Do not add runtime plugin execution to M1.
Do not discover plugins outside instance-admin declared roots.
Validate manifest schema and engine.dreamgraph before importing plugin main modules.
Keep ESM as the default supported plugin module target unless a later ADR supersedes it.
Do not imply in-process plugin loading is sandboxed before worker isolation exists.

decisions.title: Schedule actions will migrate from a closed union to a guarded registry without changing existing schedule semantics

context.problem: The SDK roadmap requires plugins to eventually register schedule action types, but current schedule behavior depends on known built-in actions, timeout handling, error streaks, and workflow visibility. Opening the action type space without a registry design could break existing schedule semantics or make custom actions unobservable.
constraints: Existing built-in schedule semantics must not change during registry migration.
Timeout and error-streak guards must apply uniformly to built-in and plugin actions.
system://workflows must continue to expose a stable enumerable surface for operators and tools.
Plugin actions must be capability-gated and schema-validated.
M4 implements the seam; M1 should only document and type the eventual contract where needed.
related_tensions: Open plugin seams must not weaken core operational guards
SDK contracts should avoid freezing implementation internals too early

decision.chosen: Adopt a schedule action registry design in which built-ins are first-class registry entries, plugin actions use open string IDs only through explicit registration, every action declares a zod-validated parameter schema, and the scheduler invokes all action types through the same timeout, error-streak, and observability wrapper. system://workflows lists both built-in and registered plugin action metadata while preserving stable built-in identifiers.

alternatives.option: Keep ScheduleAction as a permanently closed union
alternatives.rejected_because: Prevents the planned plugin schedule action seam.

alternatives.option: Allow arbitrary string actions without a registry
alternatives.rejected_because: Breaks validation, observability, and operator trust.

alternatives.option: Give plugin actions a separate scheduler path
alternatives.rejected_because: Would bypass or duplicate timeout/error-streak behavior and create inconsistent semantics.

expected: M4 can open the schedule action seam without bypassing existing protections.
Built-in actions can migrate incrementally into the registry.
Operators retain a discoverable action catalog.
Plugin action failures produce the same telemetry and pause behavior as built-in failures.
risks: Registry migration may reveal assumptions in code that expects a closed union.
Action ID collision rules must be precise to avoid shadowing built-ins.
Schema validation errors need clear operator-facing rejection reasons.

guard_rails: Do not invoke plugin schedule actions outside the shared scheduler guard wrapper.
Do not allow plugin action IDs to collide with built-in action IDs.
Require registered action parameter schemas before accepting a schedule using a plugin action.
Keep built-in action IDs stable in system://workflows.
Do not implement arbitrary string action execution without registry metadata.

decisions.title: M3 plugin host runtime is now active and graph should treat plugin loading as implemented, tested platform capability

context.problem: The project has moved beyond the M1/M2 planning state for plugins. M3 host runtime, stable plugin telemetry contracts, reject reasons, system://plugins inventory, dg plugin CLI, and reference plugin loading are now implemented and tested, but prior graph knowledge and ADR context still emphasize future-tense or host-stub assumptions. The graph must preserve the milestone transition so future reasoning does not continue treating plugin loading as unimplemented.
constraints: Plugin loading in M3 is in-process and trust-gated; it is not a sandbox.
The host runtime is opt-in via allowInProcessPlugins / DG_ALLOW_INPROCESS_PLUGINS and may also require per-plugin trust.
Stable plugin telemetry kinds are host-owned contracts and must remain documented as such.
system://plugins is the canonical operator-visible inventory for loaded/discovered plugins.
Runtime evidence from server logs confirms at least one successful plugin load for examples.hello-events@0.1.0.

decision.chosen: Treat M3 as completed and update graph reasoning accordingly: @dreamgraph/host is an implemented daemon plugin runtime providing discovery, manifest validation, capability/effect gating, telemetry emission, trust banner behavior, watchdog support, system://plugins inventory, and dg plugin administration. Plugin telemetry event kinds and PluginRejectReason are stable SDK contracts. examples/hello-events is the reference plugin and runtime evidence of successful loading should be considered validation input for the feature state.

alternatives.option: Keep graph state at pre-M3 planning/stub status until a later manual documentation sweep
alternatives.rejected_because: This leaves the graph stale and causes future reasoning to misclassify implemented host-runtime behavior as planned-only.

alternatives.option: Treat M3 plugin runtime as production-sandboxed capability
alternatives.rejected_because: The current model is trust-gated in-process execution, not worker-isolated sandboxing; overstating security would be inaccurate.

expected: Future graph queries can rely on plugin host runtime as implemented rather than speculative.
Operator/runtime reasoning can use system://plugins and dg plugin as active surfaces.
Future planning can treat worker isolation and deeper sandboxing as later milestones rather than prerequisites for plugin loading existence.
risks: Some pre-existing graph entities and docs may still contain stale future-tense wording until separately refreshed.
Recording milestone completion via ADR does not by itself rewrite every feature/workflow entity description.

guard_rails: Do not describe M3 plugin execution as sandboxed; it is trust-gated in-process loading until later worker isolation lands.
Do not regress plugin telemetry kinds from stable host-owned SDK contracts without a superseding ADR.
Do not model webhook dead-letter as part of M3 plugin host completion; that remains outside this milestone.

decisions.title: Cards are split by responsibility: DreamGraph persists task state, webview owns UI state, cards are views not entities

context.problem: v1 Architect mixes card responsibilities: the webview parses LLM JSON envelopes itself (third copy of extraction logic), some task state is implicit in chat history with no separate record, and cognitive cycles cannot reason over past task outcomes because they are not persisted as graph entities. The team needs a clean split that preserves graph-grounded reasoning while letting the UI evolve freely.
constraints: Task history must survive extension reload, workspace reload, and multi-session work — it is durable evidence.
UI presentation must evolve freely without migrating persisted data.
Cognitive cycles (dreams, tensions, narrative) must be able to reason over past task outcomes.
Webview must not become a parallel parsing surface for LLM envelopes — today's three-extractor problem must not recur.

decision.chosen: Cards are split by responsibility. DreamGraph persists task-state records: decisions taken, blockers encountered, verification evidence, graph-linked context summaries, autonomy pass outcomes, provider+model used, and tool-call results that have lasting value. The VS Code webview owns rendered card UI state: layout, expand/collapse, streaming progress, transient presentation, animation timing, and per-instance preferences. Cards are views over persisted task records, not graph entities themselves. The webview consumes typed events emitted by the orchestrator and never re-parses LLM envelopes directly.

alternatives.option: Cards as full graph entities
alternatives.rejected_because: Couples graph schema to UI presentation churn; every webview redesign would mutate persisted graph data, and the graph would carry rendering noise (collapse states, scroll positions) that has no semantic value.

alternatives.option: Cards owned entirely by webview
alternatives.rejected_because: Loses durable task history; reload, multi-session continuity, and graph-grounded reasoning over past decisions would all be impossible because the webview is ephemeral and unreachable from cognitive cycles.

alternatives.option: Mirror everything to both stores
alternatives.rejected_because: Doubles persistence cost and creates synchronization bugs; every UI tweak risks corrupting graph state and every graph update risks mis-rendering.

expected: Task history is queryable via DreamGraph for audit, narrative, and dream-cycle reasoning.
Webview redesign is a presentation-only change with zero persistence migration.
Single canonical envelope extractor in architect-v2/cards/ — the three-parallel-extractors problem from v1 cannot recur because the webview consumes typed events instead of raw text.
Cards display correctly across all providers, all streaming states, and all partial-response edge cases because rendering reads from a single typed source.
risks: Graph schema must accommodate task-state records (new entity type or extension of existing); requires careful design.
Typed event protocol between orchestrator and webview becomes a stable contract that must be versioned.
Initial implementation cost is higher than 'webview parses everything' but pays back in reliability and graph reasoning.

guard_rails: Do not parse LLM envelopes inside the webview — it consumes only typed events from the orchestrator.
Do not store UI presentation state (collapse, scroll, animation) in DreamGraph.
Do not store durable task evidence (decisions, blockers, verification, provider, model) only in the webview.
Do not introduce a second envelope extractor anywhere in architect-v2/; the canonical extractor lives in architect-v2/cards/.
Do not let webview state and graph task records drift — graph is authoritative for what happened, webview is authoritative only for how it currently looks.

decisions.title: Architect v2 enforces a strict 5-tier execution priority: MCP graph → MCP mutation → MCP verification → VS Code APIs → shell

context.problem: v1 Architect's tool execution layer has implicit precedence between local extension-host tools and MCP daemon tools, with name collisions (local write_file vs MCP create_file, local read_local_file vs MCP read_source_code) and bypass points where v1 reaches for vscode.workspace.fs / vscode.workspace.findFiles when an MCP/DreamGraph tool would be the graph-first choice. Without a structural priority order, graph-first is a slogan, not an invariant.
constraints: Graph-first principle: DreamGraph is the primary context, planning, memory, and safety boundary — reaching around it must be the exception, not the default.
Tool selection must achieve 99.999999% reliability target with no false 'tool unavailable' aborts.
Some operations are genuinely extension-host-only (clipboard, shell, opening editor tabs, accessing user selection) and a pure-MCP rule would be unworkable.
Today's local tools (read_local_file, write_file, modify_entity) duplicate MCP equivalents and create collisions — must be eliminated.

decision.chosen: Architect v2 enforces a single execution priority order that the tool dispatcher must follow for every tool call: (1) MCP entity / API / graph queries, (2) MCP file mutation (create_file, edit_file, edit_entity, patch_markdown_chapter), (3) MCP verification + runtime senses (query_self_metrics, query_runtime_metrics, query_db_schema, etc.), (4) VS Code editor APIs (only when MCP is genuinely inappropriate or absent for the operation), (5) generic shell via run_command. The dispatcher logs the selected tier per call as machine-readable trace. Local 'duplicate' tools (read_local_file, write_file, modify_entity) are removed; only operations that genuinely require the extension host (clipboard, shell, opening editor tabs for the user, document selection) remain at tier 4. Any code path that flips this priority must escalate via a new ADR.

alternatives.option: Keep v1's mixed local+MCP tool registry as-is
alternatives.rejected_because: Today's tool collisions (local write_file vs MCP create_file, etc.) and unclear precedence cause silent behavior changes when MCP availability flips; this is exactly the patch-stacking smell the rewrite must eliminate.

alternatives.option: Pure MCP, no local fallback
alternatives.rejected_because: Some operations (clipboard access, shell execution against the user's workspace) are extension-host-only capabilities that the daemon genuinely cannot provide; a pure-MCP rule would force unnatural detours.

alternatives.option: Let the LLM decide priority case-by-case
alternatives.rejected_because: Violates the 99.999999% tool-selection reliability target; relies on prompt discipline rather than structural enforcement, and the LLM's choice would be invisible to audit.

expected: MCP/DreamGraph is structurally privileged in every tool call; graph-first is enforced by the dispatcher, not by prompt discipline.
Tool-selection trace is machine-readable and auditable per call — future drift is detectable.
Tool collisions disappear because local duplicates of MCP tools are removed; only extension-host-unique operations remain at tier 4.
Adding a new tool requires explicit tier assignment, making the priority order self-documenting.
risks: Some MCP tools may have higher latency than local equivalents; users may notice slower file operations. Mitigation: cache hot reads at the dispatcher tier, not at the tool tier.
Tier 4 boundary judgments (when is VS Code API genuinely required?) need consistent enforcement during code review.
Removing local duplicates means MCP availability becomes a hard dependency; daemon down = degraded experience. Mitigation: clear UX signal when MCP is unreachable.

guard_rails: Do not call a VS Code editor API for an operation an MCP tool can perform.
Do not reintroduce local duplicates of MCP file-mutation tools (write_file, edit_file, edit_entity, etc.).
Do not bypass the dispatcher to call a tool directly — all calls flow through the prioritized registry.
Do not skip the tier-trace log for any tool invocation.
Do not flip the tier order for a single call without recording a new ADR.

decisions.title: Architect v2 locks local provider flagships: LM Studio = gpt-oss-120b high-context, Ollama = qwen2.5-coder:32b

context.problem: v1 Architect leaves local provider model selection entirely to user settings, which produces ambiguous first-run behavior for LM Studio and Ollama users and complicates documentation, benchmarking, and troubleshooting because there is no canonical 'recommended' model per provider.
constraints: Local-first deployments need a sensible flagship default per provider; first-run experience with no model picked is poor.
LM Studio and Ollama have different runtime characteristics; a single shared default would be wrong for at least one.
User explicitly chose these flagships during the rewrite kickoff and locked them as the v2 baseline.
Cloud provider defaults must stay aligned with the v9.0.0 locked set (GPT-5.5/5.4, Claude 4.7 xhigh).

decision.chosen: Architect v2 ships with locked local provider flagships: LM Studio default model = gpt-oss-120b in high-context configuration. Ollama default model = qwen2.5-coder:32b. These are the recommended defaults baked into the provider profile model; users override per-instance via settings, but the out-of-box experience uses these flagships. Cloud provider defaults (already locked in v9.0.0): OpenAI = GPT-5.5 Responses API as default + GPT-5.4 previous API as equal-class option; Anthropic = Claude 4.7 xhigh.

alternatives.option: Leave local provider defaults as 'whatever the user has installed'
alternatives.rejected_because: Settings ambiguity wastes user time; first-run experience with LM Studio or Ollama is poor when no flagship is recommended, and the user explicitly asked for locked defaults.

alternatives.option: Make local providers a single shared default
alternatives.rejected_because: LM Studio and Ollama have different runtime characteristics and different best-in-class models; a shared default would be wrong for at least one of them.

alternatives.option: Auto-detect installed local model and pick the best one at runtime
alternatives.rejected_because: Adds discovery logic and surprise; users prefer predictable defaults they can override over magic that might pick the wrong model.

expected: First-run experience with LM Studio or Ollama is predictable: a flagship is selected, user knows what to download.
Provider profile model can ship validated capability flags for these specific defaults (context window, tool-call format, reasoning support).
Documentation, troubleshooting, and benchmark suites can target known defaults rather than 'whatever the user picked'.
Users override defaults per-instance via VS Code settings; the lock is only for out-of-box experience.
risks: Recommended local flagships may become outdated as new models release; superseding ADR will be required when bumping defaults.

User hardware may not support the flagship (gpt-oss-120b high-context needs significant VRAM); UX must clearly signal hardware requirements and provide fallback guidance without silently switching models.

guard_rails: Do not change the LM Studio default away from gpt-oss-120b high-context without a superseding ADR.
Do not change the Ollama default away from qwen2.5-coder:32b without a superseding ADR.
Do not change cloud provider defaults (GPT-5.5 Responses API + GPT-5.4 previous API + Claude 4.7 xhigh) without a superseding ADR.
Do not silently fall back to a different local model when the flagship is unavailable — surface the gap clearly so the user can install or override.

decisions.title: Architect v2 providers are profile records in a registry; orchestrator depends only on the ProviderAdapter contract

context.problem: Architect v1 routes provider-specific behavior through switch statements inside `ArchitectLlm`, hardcodes model capability flags, and parses tool-call envelopes in multiple places. Inventory \u00a71.4, \u00a72 row 6, and \u00a75 row \"Provider model-list rot\" identify this as a structural cause of the two-OpenAI-paths smell, the silent reasoning-effort header risk, and adapter divergence. v2 needs a uniform abstraction that the orchestrator and autonomy engine can depend on without ever knowing which provider is active.
constraints: Architect v2 must remain provider-agnostic at the orchestrator layer; provider quirks may not leak past the adapter boundary.
Adding or removing a provider must be a single registry change, not a switch-case surgery across multiple files.
Tool-call reliability target (99.999999% per inventory §3) requires the canonical tool-call shape to be defined once and translated by adapters, not parsed in multiple places.
Strict isolation from v1 — no `import` and no copy-paste of v1 provider code (locked at Slice 2 kickoff).

decision.chosen: Architect v2 models providers as `ProviderProfile` records in a registry rather than a class hierarchy. Each profile declares: its `id` (closed enum), `displayName`, `modelSource` ('static' or 'discovery'), `defaultModelId`, `listModels()`, and `createAdapter(model, config)`. Each model is a `ModelDescriptor` with declarative `ModelCapabilities` (api discriminator, streaming, toolCallShape, attachments, reasoning support, maxOutputTokens). The orchestrator depends only on the `ProviderAdapter` contract (`stream`, `callWithTools`) and the canonical request/response/event/error shapes \u2014 it never branches on provider id at the wire layer. Slice 2 ships the types + registry + stub adapters that throw `ProviderAdapterNotImplementedError`; real adapters land in later slices behind the v2 feature flag.

alternatives.option: Keep v1's class-based ArchitectLlm shape and just rebuild internals
alternatives.rejected_because: v1's switch-statement provider routing is the root cause of the two-OpenAI-paths smell and the silent reasoning-effort header mismatch risks documented in inventory §1.4 and §5; a per-provider record-based registry is what makes ADR-148 (one OpenAI provider, model-driven dispatch) implementable cleanly.

alternatives.option: Use a third-party LLM router library (LangChain.js / Vercel AI SDK)
alternatives.rejected_because: Adds a heavy runtime dependency, hides the provider quirks behind another abstraction we'd still have to debug, and conflicts with the rewrite principle of owning the wire layer end-to-end for token economy and tool-call reliability.

alternatives.option: Defer the registry until after a working adapter exists
alternatives.rejected_because: Slice 3+ work (autonomy, execution) needs a stable seam to depend on; without the registry contract, every later slice would re-invent its own adapter abstraction and we would re-create v1's tangled state.

expected: Future slices implement their own logic against the `ProviderAdapter` contract; they can be developed and tested with mock adapters before any provider is wired.
Adding a fifth provider (e.g. xAI, Google) becomes a single new profile file plus one registry entry, not a refactor of `ArchitectLlm`.
The two-OpenAI-paths smell from v1 inventory §2 row 6 is structurally precluded — model.capabilities.api is the single source of truth for wire format.

Capability flags drive request shaping declaratively; the silent reasoning-effort header risk from inventory §5 cannot recur because unknown effort levels are caught by `ReasoningSupport.effortLevels` enforcement at the adapter boundary.
risks: The canonical `ChatRequest` / `StreamEvent` / `ToolCall` shapes must absorb every provider's quirks; a future provider with truly novel semantics may force a backwards-incompatible widening.

Stub adapters are runtime-throwing; if a code path accidentally instantiates a stub during Slice 2 work it will fail at the call site (mitigated: feature flag remains off and stub adapters are easy to recognize in stack traces).
Discovery-source providers (LM Studio, Ollama) ship Slice-2 placeholder lists; consumers that enumerate models must understand this is not yet the real list.

guard_rails: Do not branch on `ProviderId` inside the orchestrator or autonomy engine — branch on `ModelCapabilities` fields.
Do not introduce a provider-specific request type that bypasses `ChatRequest`; adapters translate from the canonical shape, not from a per-provider one.
Do not parse provider-specific tool-call envelopes anywhere except the corresponding adapter; the rest of v2 sees only `ToolCall`.
Do not throw provider-raw errors past the adapter boundary; every failure must be wrapped in `ProviderError` with a closed-enum `kind`.
Do not ship a provider adapter without the corresponding `ModelCapabilities` flags being honored end-to-end (streaming, toolCallShape, reasoning, attachments).

decisions.title: Single 'openai' provider; ModelCapabilities.api selects Chat Completions vs Responses API per model

context.problem: v1 ships two parallel OpenAI code paths \u2014 standard Chat Completions in `architect-llm.ts` and Responses API in `openai-responses-adapter.ts`. Inventory flags this as a HIGH-MEDIUM duplication smell. v2 must support both APIs (because gpt-5.5 requires Responses API while older models still use Chat Completions) without reproducing the dual-path problem.
constraints: v1's two parallel OpenAI paths (architect-llm.ts standard route + openai-responses-adapter.ts) are a HIGH-MEDIUM smell in inventory §2 row 6; v2 must not reproduce them at the provider-id level.
Users select a model, not an API; the UX must match.
OpenAI's roster includes both Chat Completions models and Responses-API-only models simultaneously, so a single-API-per-provider model is incorrect.
The dispatch decision must be declarative on the model descriptor, not buried inside adapter code.

decision.chosen: Architect v2 exposes ONE `openai` provider entry. Each model's `ModelCapabilities.api` field is the discriminator that selects between OpenAI Chat Completions and OpenAI Responses API at request time. Slice 2 wires gpt-5.5 with `api: 'openai-responses'` and gpt-5.4 with `api: 'openai-chat-completions'`. The orchestrator never sees an 'OpenAI mode' selector; users pick a model, and the model's metadata routes the request.

alternatives.option: Two distinct providers: 'openai-chat' and 'openai-responses'
alternatives.rejected_because: Splits the OpenAI surface in the settings UI and forces users to think about which API a model uses; this is exactly the cognitive leak ADR-148 exists to remove. It also recreates the v1 two-paths smell at a higher level.

alternatives.option: Hardcode an api branch inside one OpenAI adapter implementation (no capability flag)
alternatives.rejected_because: Pushes the provider-specific switch one level deeper instead of removing it; the orchestrator would still need to know which OpenAI 'mode' it was talking to in order to handle reasoning round-trip semantics correctly.

alternatives.option: Auto-detect API per model from id naming conventions ('gpt-5*' → responses)
alternatives.rejected_because: Naming conventions are not a contract; OpenAI has changed model id conventions before and may again. A declarative capability flag on the descriptor is robust to future renames.

expected: Settings UI shows a unified 'OpenAI' provider with all models in one list.
Adding a new OpenAI model (e.g. a future Responses-API-only release) is one entry in `OPENAI_MODELS` with the correct `api` flag; no code branches change.
The v1 inventory §2 row 6 'Two OpenAI paths' smell is structurally extinct in v2.
Per-model behavior (reasoning round-trip, encrypted_content for Responses) is encapsulated inside the OpenAI adapter implementation, gated on `model.capabilities.api`.
risks: The OpenAI adapter implementation must contain a clean per-`api` dispatch internally; if it grows undisciplined it will become a smaller version of the v1 ArchitectLlm.
If OpenAI introduces a third API surface, the `ModelApi` enum must be widened and the adapter must add a third internal branch.

guard_rails: Do not introduce a second OpenAI-family entry in the registry (e.g. 'openai-responses', 'openai-classic'); the registry has exactly one `openai` provider.
Do not branch on model id strings to choose the API; branch on `model.capabilities.api`.
Do not allow an OpenAI model descriptor without a populated `capabilities.api` field.
Do not hardcode Responses-API-specific shapes (encrypted_content, output array) outside the OpenAI adapter.

decisions.title: Hybrid model-list source: TS const tables for cloud providers, runtime discovery for local providers

context.problem: Inventory \u00a75 flags 'Provider model-list rot' as a v1 risk: hardcoded `ANTHROPIC_MODELS` and `OPENAI_MODELS` arrays go stale, while local providers (LM Studio, Ollama) host different models on different user machines and cannot be enumerated statically at all. A single mechanism cannot serve both.
constraints: Cloud provider model lists are stable and benefit from compile-time validation.
Local provider model rosters are user-specific and change frequently as users pull/delete models.
Default model resolution must work at extension activation without requiring network calls (per Slice 2 verification criterion 3-6).
Inventory §5 risk 'Provider model-list rot' must be addressed for cloud providers without imposing release friction on local-provider users.

decision.chosen: Architect v2 uses a hybrid model-list source. Cloud providers (`openai`, `anthropic`) ship their model lists as TypeScript const tables in `providers/openai.ts` and `providers/anthropic.ts` \u2014 type-checked, versioned with code, requires a release to add a model. Local providers (`lmstudio`, `ollama`) declare `modelSource: 'discovery'` and obtain their model lists at runtime via the provider's own discovery endpoint (LM Studio `/v1/models`, Ollama `/api/tags`). Slice 2 ships the discovery seam only; the Slice 2 `listModels()` for local providers returns a single-entry list containing the locked default (ADR-145) so the registry resolves consistently without network. Slice 3+ replaces the seam with real fetch + caching.

alternatives.option: TS const tables for all four providers
alternatives.rejected_because: Local providers (LM Studio, Ollama) host different models on different user machines; shipping a fixed list would either be wrong on most installs or require constant releases just to track local model availability.

alternatives.option: Runtime discovery for all four providers
alternatives.rejected_because: Anthropic and OpenAI publish stable model lists that benefit from compile-time type checking; calling their model-listing endpoints on every session adds latency and a new failure mode for no benefit.

alternatives.option: Single JSON file shipped with the extension
alternatives.rejected_because: Solves neither half of the problem cleanly: cloud lists lose type-checking; local lists still need runtime discovery to be correct per-install.

expected: Cloud users get type-checked model lists with capability flags validated at build time.
Local users get a model list that reflects what they actually have installed.
Discovery failures degrade gracefully — the locked default is always present even if discovery returns nothing.
Adding a new cloud model is a typed code change with full IDE assistance; adding a new local model requires no extension change at all.
risks: Two code paths for model listing increase surface area; contract tests must verify both paths satisfy the same `ProviderProfile.listModels()` interface.
Discovery endpoints can fail; the orchestrator must handle empty/error results gracefully (currently mitigated by always including the locked default).
Local discovery requires network access to localhost; sandboxed environments that block this will see only the locked default.

guard_rails: Do not introduce a static const model table for `lmstudio` or `ollama` (beyond the locked-default fallback in Slice 2).
Do not rely on runtime discovery for `openai` or `anthropic`; their lists are part of the build.
Do not let a discovery failure remove the locked default from the resolved list — the default must always be reachable.
Do not cache discovered model lists indefinitely; future slices must implement an explicit TTL and refresh semantics.

decisions.title: Cloud provider defaults locked: OpenAI gpt-5.5 (Responses) + gpt-5.4 (Chat) equal-class; Anthropic claude-4.7 xhigh

context.problem: ADR-145 locked the local-provider flagship defaults (LM Studio gpt-oss-120b high-context, Ollama qwen2.5-coder:32b) but did not name the cloud-provider flagship defaults. Slice 2 needs these locked too, both so first-run users land on a quality default and so verification can assert them mechanically.
constraints: ADR-145 locked local-provider defaults but left cloud defaults implicit; this ADR closes that gap.
First-run users must land on a deliberate, high-quality default without any settings interaction.
Defaults must be mechanically discoverable so verification (Slice 2 §6 criteria 3-4) can assert them.

decision.chosen: Architect v2 cloud provider defaults are explicitly locked. OpenAI flagship default = `gpt-5.5` via Responses API. OpenAI equal-class second = `gpt-5.4` via Chat Completions (previous API). Anthropic flagship default = `claude-4.7` with `defaultEffort: 'xhigh'`. These values are encoded as `defaultModelId` on each provider profile and as `defaultEffort` inside the model's `ReasoningSupport`. Settings may override per-user; the registry-level default may not be silently changed.

alternatives.option: Defer cloud defaults to user settings only
alternatives.rejected_because: Reproduces the v1 ambiguity inventory §5 calls out; new users with no settings would land on whatever the registry lists first, which is implicit and brittle.

alternatives.option: Always default to the cheapest model in each provider
alternatives.rejected_because: The Architect rewrite explicitly targets quality and tool-call reliability; defaulting to a weaker model would systematically degrade out-of-box behavior to save cost the user did not opt into.

alternatives.option: Default to the most recent model id at registry-build time
alternatives.rejected_because: Couples defaults to release timing rather than to a deliberate quality choice; would silently change defaults on every cloud release that adds a newer id.

expected: First-run experience for cloud providers matches the rewrite's quality intent without any user configuration.
Slice 2 verification can assert defaults by inspection of the registry.
Future cloud-default changes require an explicit superseding ADR, not a quiet model-list edit.
risks: Cloud providers occasionally rename or sunset model ids; the lock will need a superseding ADR if `gpt-5.5` or `claude-4.7` is renamed/retired.
Defaulting to high-effort reasoning (Anthropic xhigh) increases per-request cost; this is intentional for quality but should be visible to cost-conscious users via settings.

guard_rails: Do not change `defaultModelId` for `openai` away from `gpt-5.5` without a superseding ADR.
Do not change `defaultModelId` for `anthropic` away from `claude-4.7` without a superseding ADR.
Do not change Anthropic's `defaultEffort` away from `xhigh` without a superseding ADR.
Do not silently demote a default to a cheaper model id; cost-driven defaults require explicit user opt-in.

decisions.title: Architect v2 autonomy is a pure deriveNextAction() function returning a DecisionResult discriminated union

context.problem: v1 autonomy spreads decision logic across `autonomy.ts`, `autonomy-loop.ts`, `autonomy-structured.ts`, and `autonomy-contract.ts`. Mode-specific behavior is encoded as switch branches inside `chooseActionForMode` and `shouldContinueAfterPass`, mixed with empty-pass heuristics and pass-envelope parsing. Inventory \u00a71.5 lists this as the LARGEST single tangle in v1. v2 needs a single pure decision function so the rest of the rewrite has one stable seam to depend on.
constraints: Same inputs MUST always produce the same `DecisionResult` (replayability for debugging and auditing).
The decision module must be provider-agnostic — no import from `architect-v2/providers/`.
Slice 4 (MCP-first execution) needs a stable `CapabilityInventory` interface to plug into.
Slices 5–7 each consume a distinct piece of this contract; the shape must accommodate them without breaking changes.

decision.chosen: Architect v2 autonomy is a pure function `deriveNextAction(taskState, inventory, candidates, now) -> DecisionResult`. `DecisionResult` is a discriminated union: `{ kind: 'continue', need: ContinuationNeed } | { kind: 'pause_for_user', reason, ranked, note } | { kind: 'stop', condition: StopCondition }`. The function reads `TaskState` (mode, profile, passes, blockers, budgets, status), the `CapabilityInventory`, and a list of `ActionCandidate`s; it never calls a provider, never mutates state, never performs I/O. The orchestrator owns state transitions and pass execution; the autonomy module owns only the decision.

alternatives.option: Port v1 `shouldContinueAfterPass` rule cascade verbatim
alternatives.rejected_because: v1's cascade entangles mode-specific branching with budget checks, scope checks, empty-pass heuristics, and uncertainty enums in a single function. The user directive at Slice 3 kickoff was 'carry only the concept and the settings' — not the implementation. Porting verbatim would re-import the architecture this rewrite exists to remove.

alternatives.option: Make `deriveNextAction` an event-emitting class with internal state
alternatives.rejected_because: Hidden state breaks reproducibility — we can't replay a decision from a `TaskState` snapshot if the engine carries its own state across calls. Pure function with explicit inputs is auditable and trivially testable.

alternatives.option: Defer the decision contract to Slice 5 (cards) where the UI integration lives
alternatives.rejected_because: Every later slice (MCP execution, cards, capability matrix, verification harness) consumes some part of this contract. Defining it now lets all four be designed against the same seam.

expected: Decisions are testable as plain function calls with literal `TaskState` fixtures.
Bug reports can include a `TaskState` snapshot and a `nowEpochMs` and be reproduced exactly.
Slices 4–7 each plug into a stable seam without negotiating new contracts.
Removing v1 `autonomy*.ts` at the v10 cutover is a single deletion + import flip, not a coordinated multi-file refactor.
risks: The discriminated union may need to widen as Slices 4–7 surface new requirements; widening is OK, narrowing is a breaking change.

If `CapabilityInventory` from Slice 4 turns out to need async lookup, the function signature widens to async — mitigated by keeping the Slice 3 stub synchronous and asserting that capabilities are pre-resolved before `deriveNextAction` is called.
Pure-function discipline requires callers to pass `nowEpochMs` rather than calling `Date.now()` inside; missing this in callers re-introduces hidden non-determinism.

guard_rails: Do not add I/O (network, disk, terminal, vscode API) inside the autonomy module.
Do not mutate any input to `deriveNextAction`; the function is pure.
Do not move state transitions into the autonomy module — the orchestrator owns them.
Do not import from `architect-v2/providers/` inside `architect-v2/autonomy/`.
Do not bypass `createContinuationNeed()` to construct a `ContinuationNeed` literal — the constructor enforces ADR-154.

decisions.title: Autonomy modes preserved by name (cautious, conscientious, eager, autonomous); semantics rebuilt as a MODE_PROFILES data table

context.problem: v1 autonomy modes are defined by per-mode code branches inside `chooseActionForMode` and `shouldContinueAfterPass`. The behavioral difference between modes is invisible without reading both functions in parallel. The user directive at Slice 3 kickoff was to keep the v1 setting names but rebuild the semantics around explicit knobs.
constraints: v1 mode names must remain the user-facing labels (Slice 3 carry-over).
Adding a fifth mode in the future should be one row in the table plus widening the `AutonomyMode` union, NOT a refactor.
Tuning thresholds to telemetry must not require code changes outside `modes.ts`.
All four modes must remain meaningfully distinct — each row's knob values differ from every other row in at least three of the five columns.

decision.chosen: Architect v2 keeps the four v1 mode names verbatim (`cautious`, `conscientious`, `eager`, `autonomous`) as the user-facing setting. Mode SEMANTICS are rebuilt from scratch as a `MODE_PROFILES` data table whose rows declare exactly five knobs: `defaultPassBudget`, `defaultTimeBudgetMs`, `confidenceThreshold`, `blockerTolerance`, `verificationStrictness`. No code anywhere in v2 branches on the mode enum directly \u2014 every consumer reads a knob value off `getModeProfile(mode)`. Initial calibration: cautious=(3 passes, 2 min, 0.95, 0, strict); conscientious=(8, 5 min, 0.85, 0, strict); eager=(20, 10 min, 0.70, 1, normal); autonomous=(50, 30 min, 0.55, 2, normal).

alternatives.option: Rename the modes too
alternatives.rejected_because: User directive at Slice 3 kickoff was explicit: keep the same UX labels with completely new behavior. Renaming would force users to relearn settings without delivering UX value.

alternatives.option: Keep v1's per-mode rule branches but move them into a single function
alternatives.rejected_because: Hides the same complexity in one location. Modes-as-data is structurally simpler and makes the four-way comparison legible at a glance.

alternatives.option: Drop modes entirely and expose individual knobs
alternatives.rejected_because: Violates the carry-over directive. Mode names ARE part of the v1 settings the user explicitly told us to preserve.

expected: Settings UI shows the same four labels users already know.
Behavior differences between modes are visible in one table, not scattered across switch statements.
Threshold tuning is a single-file edit (with a superseding ADR for the values).
Mode-comparison diagrams and docs auto-derive from `MODE_PROFILES`.
risks: Initial threshold calibration is a guess; real-world telemetry may show, e.g., that `eager`'s 0.70 threshold is too permissive. Mitigation: thresholds are one-line edits gated by a superseding ADR.

Wall-clock budget defaults assume reasonable provider latency; very slow providers may exhaust the time budget before the pass budget on `cautious` mode. Mitigation: both budgets are caller-overrideable.
Reducing every mode difference to five knobs may not capture future requirements (e.g. per-mode tool allowlists). Widening the row schema is the resolution path.

guard_rails: Do not add a `switch (mode)` statement anywhere in `architect-v2/`; read `MODE_PROFILES[mode]` instead.
Do not change a `MODE_PROFILES` row value without a superseding ADR — the calibration is part of the contract.
Do not introduce a fifth mode without widening `AutonomyMode` AND adding the matching `MODE_PROFILES` row in the same change.
Do not use the v1 `chooseActionForMode` or `shouldContinueAfterPass` algorithms; the `MODE_PROFILES` knobs are the only mode-driven inputs.

decisions.title: Dual budget model: PassBudget (required) + TimeBudget (defaulted per mode); both visible, both bounded, no uncapped runs

context.problem: v1's pass budget was optional \u2014 `0` or `undefined` meant uncapped \u2014 and there was no wall-clock bound at all. A pass that called a slow LLM could hang indefinitely; a model that issued many small operations could blow through resources without ever tripping a counter. The Slice 3 directive was explicit: prevent both failure modes by construction.
constraints: v1's optional `totalAuthorizedPasses` (where 0 / undefined meant 'uncapped') is rejected as unsafe — the user directive at Slice 3 kickoff explicitly required dual bounded budgets.
Counters must remain visible during runs (Slice 3 carry-over: 'visible counters as a product requirement').
The decision engine must be able to detect exhaustion without performing I/O — it is given `nowEpochMs` as an input.
Both budgets must be constructible without I/O so they can be created in tests.

decision.chosen: Every Architect v2 autonomous run is bounded by BOTH a `PassBudget` AND a `TimeBudget`. `PassBudget.total` is REQUIRED on every run \u2014 there is no uncapped mode. `TimeBudget.totalMs` is defaulted per `ModeProfile.defaultTimeBudgetMs` and overrideable per run. The decision engine stops on whichever exhausts first, returning `{ kind: 'stop', condition: 'pass_budget_exhausted' }` or `{ kind: 'stop', condition: 'time_budget_exhausted' }` respectively. Both budgets expose `total` / `used` / `remaining` so the UI can display live counters at all times. `createPassBudget(0)` and `createPassBudget(NaN)` throw \u2014 there is no way to construct an unbounded run.

alternatives.option: Pass budget only (v1 model)
alternatives.rejected_because: Does not bound long-running stalls — a single pass that hangs on a slow provider call can run indefinitely while consuming zero budget. v1 had no defense against this.

alternatives.option: Time budget only
alternatives.rejected_because: Doesn't bound runaway tool-call loops within a single time window. Wall-clock alone allows pathological retry storms.

alternatives.option: Optional budgets with sensible defaults
alternatives.rejected_because: Optional means default-on which means users may not realize a long-running task is bounded; explicit-required matches the safety posture this rewrite is trying to establish.

expected: Infinite loops and long stalls are structurally precluded — the decision engine cannot return `{ kind: 'continue' }` past either budget.
UI always has both counters available via `deriveBudgetView()`.
Slow-provider degradation surfaces as `time_budget_exhausted` rather than as a hung session.
Settings UI must prompt for or validate a pass-budget integer at run start — there is no 'just keep going' option.
risks: Forcing a pass budget on every run adds a UX step (or a settings default lookup) that didn't exist in v1. Mitigation: each `ModeProfile` carries a `defaultPassBudget` that the orchestrator can apply silently.

Wall-clock budgets in untrusted/sandboxed clocks (clock skew, suspended laptops) may produce unexpected exhaustion. Mitigation: the engine takes `nowEpochMs` as a pure input; clock-source policy is a Slice 5+ concern.

Tight default time budgets on slow providers (e.g. local Ollama on a laptop CPU) may exhaust before the pass budget. Mitigation: `cautious=2min` and `conscientious=5min` defaults can be widened per-run by the caller.

guard_rails: Do not add a code path that bypasses `PassBudget.remaining <= 0` or `isTimeBudgetExhausted()` checks in `deriveNextAction`.
Do not introduce an 'unbounded' `PassBudget` constructor or default.
Do not let `PassBudget` mutate — use `consumePass()` to derive the next budget.
Do not call `Date.now()` inside `architect-v2/autonomy/`; accept `nowEpochMs` as input for testability.

decisions.title: Native tool catalog is the source of truth; MCP roster is queried only for liveness, never for discovery

context.problem: v1 mixed three sources of tool truth: hard-coded `tool-groups.ts` allowlists, runtime MCP `listTools()` discovery, and ad-hoc `local-tools.ts` wrappers. The agent's actual capability set on any given session was the union of all three at that moment, with no audit trail when something changed. Slice 1 \u00a71.5 flagged this as the third-largest tangle in v1.
constraints: DreamGraph tools must be treated as native, not as third-party negotiated capabilities.
Tool-name drift must be impossible — the orchestrator knows tool names from the catalog, not from a probe.
Roster outages must produce a recordable `mcp_tool_unavailable` signal, not a silent fallback.
New MCP tools shipped by the daemon must not change agent behavior until intentionally adopted via catalog edit + ADR.

decision.chosen: `NATIVE_TOOL_CATALOG` in `architect-v2/execution/catalog.ts` is the single source of truth for which tools v2 can invoke. Each entry is a frozen `ToolDescriptor` with exact `tool` name, `tier`, `intent`, and `kind`. The live MCP roster (`McpRosterProbe`) is queried at session start and used solely to mark catalog entries as available or unavailable in `ResolvedCatalog`. MCP tools present on the roster but absent from the catalog are recorded in `ResolvedCatalog.unknownRosterTools` for telemetry but never auto-promoted. Adding/removing a catalog entry requires a code change AND a superseding ADR.

alternatives.option: Discover the catalog at runtime from the live MCP roster
alternatives.rejected_because: DreamGraph tools are first-class to the agent (user directive at Slice 4 kickoff: 'they are native to it'). Discovery treats them like third-party tools the agent must negotiate with. It also breaks repeatability — a roster blip during session start would silently shrink the agent's capability set.

alternatives.option: Auto-promote unknown roster tools into the catalog
alternatives.rejected_because: Auto-promotion means a new MCP server can change the agent's behavior without an ADR or code change. That's exactly the silent-capability-drift mode this rewrite is designed to remove.

alternatives.option: Keep the catalog minimal and let the action producer name tools directly
alternatives.rejected_because: Tool-name embedding (ADR-154) requires the orchestrator to know exact tool names. Centralizing them in the catalog is the only place to enforce that consistently across action producers.

expected: Adding a new MCP tool to the daemon does not change the agent's behavior until the catalog is edited and the change is ADR-recorded — capability drift is opt-in only.
Cards and telemetry can render `unknownRosterTools` to surface 'the daemon now offers X, want to adopt it?' as an explicit prompt rather than as an invisible behavior change.
Tests can stub `McpRosterProbe` with a deterministic set; no live MCP needed.
The list of canonical tool names lives in one file, satisfying ADR-154's 'exact tool name' invariant by construction.
risks: Catalog can drift from the live MCP roster — if the daemon renames a tool, the catalog entry becomes a dead reference until updated. Mitigation: `ResolvedCatalog` flags it as `unavailable` and `selectExecutor` raises `NoExecutorAvailable` rather than silently misrouting.
Catalog requires manual maintenance for every MCP daemon release. Mitigation: this is a feature, not a cost — the friction is the point.
If the catalog is incomplete, the agent will under-use the MCP surface. Mitigation: `unknownRosterTools` telemetry surfaces gaps.

guard_rails: Do not auto-promote `ResolvedCatalog.unknownRosterTools` into `NATIVE_TOOL_CATALOG`. Adoption is a code change.
Do not add a catalog entry without an ADR mentioning the new tool.
Do not remove a catalog entry without a deprecating ADR.
Do not query the MCP roster outside `inventory.resolveCatalog()`. The roster is liveness data, not discovery data.
Do not let `ToolDescriptor.tool` be a label or alias — it must be the exact dispatch name (cross-cuts ADR-154).

decisions.title: selectExecutor walks T1\u2192T5 in strict order; fallbacks across tiers require an explicit FallbackJustification

context.problem: Foundation plan \u00a73 mandates a 5-tier execution priority (DreamGraph MCP knowledge \u2192 mutation \u2192 verification \u2192 VS Code editor \u2192 shell) and the user directive at Slice 4 kickoff reinforces it: 'It will naturally fall back to VS Code tools when it proves necessary and only then.' v1 had no enforcement \u2014 tool selection was ad-hoc per call site.
constraints: DreamGraph tier (T1–T3) wins over fallback tier (T4–T5) by construction — not by score, not by config.
Every fallback must carry a recordable, machine-readable reason.
A missing capability must surface as a blocker, not as a substitute tool.
Selection must be a pure function of intent + resolved catalog — same inputs, same plan, every time.

decision.chosen: `selectExecutor(intent, resolvedCatalog)` walks `TIER_ORDER` (T1 \u2192 T5) in strict ascending order. The first tier with at least one available descriptor matching the intent wins. Within a winning tier, the first descriptor in catalog declaration order wins. If the chosen tier is numerically higher than `preferredTierForIntent(intent)`, an explicit `FallbackJustification` is attached describing why (`mcp_tool_failed`, `mcp_tool_unavailable`, `intent_not_covered_by_dreamgraph`, or `editor_native_required`). If no tier covers the intent, returns `NoExecutorAvailable` which the orchestrator translates into a Slice 3 `Blocker` of kind `'capability_missing'`.

alternatives.option: Score-based selection across all tiers
alternatives.rejected_because: Scores hide the priority. A high-confidence VS Code tool could outscore a slightly-lower-confidence DreamGraph tool, which violates the 'DreamGraph first, naturally' directive. Strict ordering makes the invariant visible.

alternatives.option: Per-mode tier overrides (e.g. autonomous mode allows shell more freely)
alternatives.rejected_because: Modes are decision-layer concerns (Slice 3 / ADR-152). Bleeding them into execution would re-create the v1 entanglement that ADR-152 exists to remove.

alternatives.option: Try the chosen tier; if it fails, silently fall back
alternatives.rejected_because: Silent fallback was a v1 failure mode — the model would think a DreamGraph tool succeeded when actually a shell command had been substituted. Failures must be recorded as `FailureOutcome` and any subsequent tier change must be an explicit orchestrator decision.

expected: The 90–100% DreamGraph-tool coverage target from the user's directive is enforced by structure: any time a fallback occurs, the orchestrator gets a justification card, not a silent substitution.
Cards can render a fallback pill with the exact reason (`'MCP unavailable'` vs `'editor-native by design'`).
Slice 6 (Copilot-plus matrix) can compute parity by scanning catalog entries, no need to invoke selection.
The `preferredTierForIntent` helper makes 'is this intent DreamGraph-native?' a one-line predicate for the rest of the system.
risks: Strict ordering may pick a slow Tier-1 tool when a faster Tier-4 tool exists. Mitigation: the action producer can declare a more specific intent that only the appropriate tier covers.
If catalog ordering within a tier is wrong, the wrong tool wins ties. Mitigation: declaration order is part of the contract; reviewer attention required when adding entries.
An unknown intent (typo) will return `NoExecutorAvailable` — loud rather than silent. Intentional, but requires the action producer to know the intent vocabulary.

guard_rails: Do not allow score-based or preference-based selection to override tier order.
Do not skip recording `FallbackJustification` when chosenTier > preferredTier.
Do not let `selectExecutor` perform I/O. It is a pure function over `ResolvedCatalog`.
Do not promote a `NoExecutorAvailable` to a different tool silently — the caller must raise a blocker.

decisions.title: ToolOutcome is the single normalized event for every tool invocation regardless of provider, tier, or kind

context.problem: v1 had several result shapes: `LocalToolResult`, `McpToolCallResult`, `StructuredPassEnvelope`, ad-hoc shell objects. Cards, autonomy, and verification each parsed each shape with provider-specific branches. The user directive at Slice 4 kickoff was explicit: 'all tool results are normalized regardless of the provider.'
constraints: Provider-specific result shapes must be normalized AT the dispatcher boundary, never leak past it.
`ArtifactRef` shape must match what Slice 3 `TaskState.artifacts` consumes (no-progress detection depends on artifact hash equality).
Verification operations must be expressible without a separate event type — they're `success` outcomes carrying `evidence`.

decision.chosen: Every tool invocation \u2014 MCP, VS Code, shell, regardless of provider \u2014 produces exactly one `ToolOutcome` value: a discriminated union of `success`, `failure`, or `partial`. Every variant carries `tool`, `tier`, `intent`, `executedAtEpochMs`, `durationMs`. `success` and `partial` carry `artifacts: ArtifactRef[]`; `success` may carry `evidence: VerificationEvidence` when the operation IS a verification step. `failure` carries `failureReason`, `recoverable`, optional `suggestedFallbackTier`. Constructors validate base fields. Cards, the autonomy decision engine, and the verification harness all consume this exact shape.

alternatives.option: Per-provider result types with a thin shared base
alternatives.rejected_because: Forces every consumer (cards, autonomy, verification) to discriminate by provider before reading the result. Inverts the directive 'normalized regardless of the provider'.

alternatives.option: Free-form result envelope (e.g. `{ raw: unknown }`)
alternatives.rejected_because: Pushes parsing onto every consumer. v1's `StructuredPassEnvelope` parsing tangle was caused by exactly this pattern.

alternatives.option: Add a fourth `kind: 'cancelled'`
alternatives.rejected_because: Cancellation is a `failure` with a specific reason; modeling it as its own kind would force every consumer to handle four cases instead of three.

expected: Slice 5 cards render `ToolOutcome` directly without provider switches.

Slice 7 verification harness reads `evidence` from any tool, not just from a dedicated verify path — 'every code change should attempt relevant verification' from foundation §Verification becomes a one-line lookup.
Provider adapters become strictly boundary-layer concerns; no part of v2 outside the adapter knows what provider produced an outcome.
The autonomy `no_progress` detector compares `artifacts` arrays directly; provider differences are invisible to it.
risks: Some MCP tool results carry rich nested data that doesn't fit cleanly into `ArtifactRef[]`. Mitigation: the dispatcher boundary is responsible for projection — it may need per-tool projection logic, but that complexity stays bounded to one place.
`recoverable: boolean` is a coarse classification; some failures are conditionally recoverable. Mitigation: `failureReason` carries the detail; `recoverable` is the orchestrator's hint only.
If a tool produces no artifacts and no evidence, it looks indistinguishable from a no-op. Intentional — the no-progress detector treats it as such.

guard_rails: Do not extend `ToolOutcome` with provider-specific fields. Provider details belong in the dispatcher boundary.
Do not add a fourth top-level `kind`; cancellation, timeout, etc. are `failure` reasons.
Do not let consumers branch on `tool` strings to extract custom data — use `artifacts` and `evidence`.
Do not bypass the constructors (`success()`, `failure()`, `partial()`); they enforce base-field invariants.

decisions.title: No fallback to a higher tier without a recorded FallbackJustification carrying one of four enumerated reasons

context.problem: v1 silently substituted shell or VS Code tools when an MCP tool was unavailable or threw. The user could not tell from the card that a fallback had occurred, and the agent could not distinguish 'DreamGraph chose VS Code' from 'DreamGraph could not reach MCP'. The user directive at Slice 4 kickoff requires this to be visible and naturally rare.
constraints: The user directive 'fall back to VS Code only when it proves necessary' must be auditable post-hoc.
Cards must show WHY a fallback occurred without consulting external state.
Tier promotion (DreamGraph → fallback) must never happen silently; tier demotion (fallback → DreamGraph) is impossible by construction.
The four reasons cover every legitimate fallback case; any new case requires a superseding ADR.

decision.chosen: When `selectExecutor` chooses a tier higher (numerically) than `preferredTierForIntent(intent)`, it MUST attach a `FallbackJustification` with one of four reasons: `'mcp_tool_unavailable'`, `'mcp_tool_failed'`, `'intent_not_covered_by_dreamgraph'`, or `'editor_native_required'`. The orchestrator records this on the `PassRecord`. When the preferred tier IS already a fallback tier (T4/T5), `'editor_native_required'` is attached so cards render the right pill. There is no code path that returns a fallback plan without a justification.

alternatives.option: Walk all 5 tiers regardless and pick the best
alternatives.rejected_because: Even with strict ordering the algorithm would still consult fallback descriptors, opening the door for accidental fallback when the DreamGraph entry is technically present-but-flaky. Stopping the walk at the first DreamGraph hit makes 'available' the binding signal.

alternatives.option: Allow fallback when MCP latency exceeds a threshold
alternatives.rejected_because: Latency-based fallback is policy that belongs to the orchestrator, not to the selector. The selector's job is to identify the canonical executor; runtime decisions about whether to retry, time out, or switch live one layer up.

alternatives.option: Treat `editor_native_required` as not-a-fallback (don't justify it)
alternatives.rejected_because: Cards still need to render a 'editor-native' pill so the user knows why a Tier-4 tool was chosen for what looks like a routine intent. Justification records that fact.

expected: The 90–100% DreamGraph-coverage target becomes measurable: count `FallbackJustification` occurrences per session, watch for clusters of `'mcp_tool_unavailable'` indicating a daemon issue, or `'intent_not_covered_by_dreamgraph'` indicating a catalog gap to close.
Cards render fallback pills with one of four reasons — user can see at a glance why VS Code/shell was used.
Telemetry can flag any session where DreamGraph fallback rate exceeds a threshold for review.
Slice 6 capability matrix uses the catalog directly; this ADR ensures runtime behavior matches what the matrix promises.
risks: A noisy MCP daemon (frequent transient failures) will produce many `mcp_tool_unavailable` justifications. Intentional — the noise is the signal that the daemon needs attention.

Producers may declare a too-narrow intent that only a Tier-4 tool covers, then claim 'editor_native_required' even when a DreamGraph tool would have served. Mitigation: catalog reviewers + Slice 6 parity matrix surface coverage gaps.

guard_rails: Do not return an `ExecutionPlan` with `tier > preferredTier` and `fallbackJustification === undefined`. The selector enforces this.
Do not invent a fifth fallback reason without a superseding ADR.
Do not let the orchestrator strip `fallbackJustification` from the `PassRecord` — it's part of the audit trail.
Do not surface a `FallbackJustification` to the model in a way that lets it dismiss the fallback as 'fine'; cards should treat it as a noteworthy event.

decisions.title: Slice 6 — Two co-equal operational modes: sparse-mode best-in-class on day one, graph-amplified additive over time, never falling

context.problem: Without an explicit two-mode contract the architect either gates on graph bootstrap (useless on day one) or treats sparse-mode as degraded (loses parity with generic agents and breaks never-fall invariant).
constraints: Sparse-mode must reach parity with generic agents on day-zero install
Graph-amplified mode is strictly additive, never a precondition
No selection path may produce pass-level failure; worst case is per-capability gap
Every operation, even sparse-mode, records back to the graph

decision.chosen: Architect v2 has exactly two operational modes at the capability layer, both first-class. (1) Sparse-mode (secondary, never failing) used when density is partial/sparse/absent AND fallback exists; uses Slice-4 T4/T5 fallback intents immediately; card carries graphBound='no'|'partial'; enrichment task queued. (2) Graph-amplified (primary) used when density is rich; mandatory graph-first path; fallback forbidden. Third state is not a mode but a declared gap: graphOnly capability + absent/sparse density => skipped with explicit gap note; pass continues. Hard invariant: no capability can fall.

alternatives.option: Single mode with graph-first only and hard failure when graph is sparse
alternatives.rejected_because: Makes day-zero install useless; breaks never-fall invariant

alternatives.option: Sparse-mode as a degraded fallback (Round 1 framing)
alternatives.rejected_because: Round 2 directive escalated sparse-mode to co-equal first-class

alternatives.option: Block on scan_project before serving any capability
alternatives.rejected_because: Gates architect on long-running graph bootstrap; breaks parity with generic agents

expected: Brand-new install ships fully working coding agent at parity with generic agents
Graph-amplified mode is strictly additive over time
No Slice 6 selection path produces pass-level failure
Slice 5 cards must render graphBound pill (yes|partial|no|gap)
Slice 7 must consume enrichmentQueue and respect skippable graphOnly capabilities
risks: Density thresholds mis-tuned -> over-prefer sparse-mode (mitigation: surface density on every card)
Graph-write side effects regress -> sparse-mode never bootstraps the graph (mitigation: record-everything ADR + Slice 7 verification)
Capability misclassified as graphOnly -> sparse installs see avoidable gaps (mitigation: review of 8 graphOnly entries)

guard_rails: chooseCapabilityPath MUST never return a kind other than 'graph-amplified' | 'sparse-mode' | 'gap'
Density 'rich' MUST produce empty allowedFallback
graphOnly capability + density 'absent'|'sparse' MUST return kind='gap'
Slice 6 modules MUST NOT import from architect-v2/providers, architect-v2/cards, or any v1 path
No Slice 6 function may be impure

decisions.title: Slice 6 — Capability matrix is a frozen typed data table; selection is a pure function over (capabilityId, density)

context.problem: Selection logic could spread capability rules across switch statements, dynamic registries, or string keys — losing auditability of the 'graph-first wins' claim and making it impossible to verify completeness against the §2 plan tables.
constraints: Matrix entries reference only Slice-4 Intent literals (compile-time validated)
All entries Object.freeze'd; no mutation at runtime
Matrix size = 42 (10+8+9+6+4+5); no duplicates by id
Exactly 8 graphOnly entries (pure-graph wins)
winRationale is short, human-readable, renders on cards

decision.chosen: CAPABILITY_MATRIX is a frozen typed array of CapabilityRecord values exported from matrix.ts. Each row carries: id (CapabilityId literal), group, graphFirst (Slice-4 Intent[]), fallback (Slice-4 Intent[]), graphOnly (boolean derived from fallback.length===0), winRationale (rendered on cards), enrichOnFallback (Intent? queued when sparse-mode runs). The matrix is the contract; the catalog (Slice 4) is the implementation. Exactly 42 entries: 10 navigation + 8 history + 9 mutation + 6 verification + 4 cognition + 5 environment, with 8 graphOnly entries.

alternatives.option: Switch statements per capability inside selection logic
alternatives.rejected_because: 42 capabilities = 42 switch arms; not auditable; impossible to render as a matrix

alternatives.option: Discover capabilities dynamically from MCP tool roster
alternatives.rejected_because: Conflates roster (Slice 4 liveness) with capability contract (Slice 6); roster changes per provider but the matrix is provider-neutral

alternatives.option: Plain JSON config
alternatives.rejected_because: Loses type safety; CapabilityRecord must reference Slice-4 Intent type checked at compile time

expected: Adding a capability is a single matrix entry + selection auto-handles it
TypeScript catches typos in Intent references at compile time
Slice 5 cards can render winRationale and group from the matrix
Slice 7 can audit coverage by iterating CAPABILITY_MATRIX
risks: Matrix grows unwieldy as capabilities multiply — mitigated by group field for grouping in renderers
Intent rename in Slice 4 breaks matrix — mitigated by TypeScript compile gate

guard_rails: CAPABILITY_MATRIX MUST stay Object.freeze'd; no runtime mutation
Adding a capability requires updating matrix.ts AND the plan §2 table in the same commit
graphOnly is derived (fallback.length===0); never set manually
All Intent references MUST exist in Slice-4 INTENT_GROUPS (TypeScript compile gate)

decisions.title: Slice 6 — Record-everything contract: every capability invocation writes back to the graph so it self-bootstraps over time

context.problem: Without a record-everything contract, sparse-mode invocations leave no trace and the graph never grows. The architect would remain forever sparse on projects that never trigger an explicit scan, contradicting the user's 'evolve with time' directive.
constraints: Enrichment is non-blocking; pass completes before enrichment runs
Enrichment uses Slice-4 Intent literals (compile-time validated)
EnrichmentTask carries capabilityId + reason for audit
Orchestrator (post-cutover) decides budget; Slice 6 only declares the queue
