Native adapter complexity is higher than a simple subprocess wrapper and requires stronger verification around context, tool authority, and streaming.

guard_rails: Do not regress Copilot CLI back to a dumb prompt-in/text-out subprocess bridge without revisiting this ADR.
Do not move Copilot-specific prompt serialization, MCP config, event parsing, or process control into provider-neutral Architect core.
Do not implement Codex CLI by blindly copying Copilot CLI internals; reuse the native-adapter principles and normalized seams while validating Codex-specific behavior.
Do not allow Copilot CLI runs to satisfy graph-grounded repository claims without DreamGraph MCP grounding or equivalent authoritative validation.
Keep Context Inspector diagnostics and normalized tool traces available for native CLI adapter runs.

decisions.title: LLM-enabled tools use connected model, daemon model, then deterministic fallback

context.problem: LLM-enabled tools need a consistent model-selection order so remediation drafting and future Taste Engine features behave predictably across Architect-connected, external LLM, daemon-only, and no-LLM contexts.
constraints: Connected Architect or external LLM contexts may already provide the best task-local model and should be used when present.
Daemon-side operation must still work outside interactive Architect contexts when dreamer or normalizer LLM configuration exists.
Tools must remain usable without any LLM provider by preserving deterministic behavior.
LLM output must remain evidence-bounded, schema-validated, and compatible with existing governance.
Daemon-side LLM temperature may vary by task because drafting, normalization, and repair planning have different creativity requirements.

decision.chosen: All LLM-enabled DreamGraph tools must select models in this order: first use the connected interactive model supplied by Architect, an external LLM, or caller context; second use the configured daemon-side LLM, choosing the appropriate dreamer or normalizer model and task-appropriate temperature; third fall back to the deterministic implementation when no LLM layer is available or validated LLM output fails.

alternatives.option: Always use daemon-side LLM configuration for tool generation
alternatives.rejected_because: This ignores richer connected Architect or external LLM contexts that may already carry the task model, user intent, and conversation-local constraints.

alternatives.option: Always use the connected Architect or external model and fail without it
alternatives.rejected_because: Daemon-side tools must remain useful in scheduled, headless, and non-interactive contexts.

alternatives.option: Replace deterministic implementations entirely once LLM drafting exists
alternatives.rejected_because: DreamGraph needs reliable no-provider operation and a validation fallback for malformed, unavailable, or low-confidence LLM output.

expected: Remediation LLM drafting will work in interactive Architect contexts, daemon-only contexts, and no-LLM contexts without changing the public get_remediation_plan contract.
Future LLM-enabled tools will share one predictable provider precedence rule instead of inventing per-tool routing.
Daemon-side tools can choose task-appropriate temperature while staying within strict schema validation and graph-governed evidence boundaries.
Observability can report which model layer was selected and why fallback occurred.
risks: Connected model behavior may vary across adapters unless the schema and validation layer stay strict.
Daemon-side temperature flexibility can make outputs less reproducible if task defaults are not documented.
Maintaining deterministic fallbacks increases implementation surface area but preserves reliability.

guard_rails: Do not make daemon-side LLM the first choice when a connected Architect, external LLM, or caller-supplied model context is available for the same LLM-enabled tool invocation.
Do not fail an LLM-enabled tool solely because no LLM is configured when a deterministic fallback exists.
Do not surface LLM-generated tool output until it passes the tool's schema, evidence, governance, and safety validation.
Do not hard-code one daemon-side temperature for all LLM-enabled tools; choose temperature per task and document defaults where behavior matters.
Do not remove existing deterministic behavior from an LLM-enabled tool without recording a replacement ADR.

decisions.title: Separate DreamGraph product semantics from repository-instance specifics

context.problem: DreamGraph can be used to assist development of its own repository, but product behavior must remain suitable for arbitrary client projects. Prompt-routing and tool-selection decisions must not treat the DreamGraph repository instance as special evidence that generic DreamGraph product concepts, such as dreams or scheduling, should be avoided or narrowed.
constraints: DreamGraph is a general product used across many client instances, not only the DreamGraph source repository.
When DreamGraph operates on its own repository, that repository is just one client workspace and must not leak project-specific assumptions into product semantics.
Tool selection should prioritize user intent and product vocabulary over defensive avoidance caused by the current workspace name.
Changes should keep minimal blast radius by updating prompt/tool-selection policy without changing runtime tool implementations unless needed.

decision.chosen: Treat DreamGraph product vocabulary, including generic terms like dream, dreaming, schedule, and scheduling, as valid routing signals independent of whether the current workspace is the DreamGraph repository. Do not suppress product-level keywords merely because they may also appear in the product or repository name.

alternatives.option: Avoid plain product terms such as dream because they may match DreamGraph in the current repository.
alternatives.rejected_because: This lets one client workspace contaminate global product behavior and makes users discover exact tool names unnecessarily.

alternatives.option: Special-case the DreamGraph repository to avoid self-reference.
alternatives.rejected_because: Special-casing the product repository increases complexity and violates the principle that DreamGraph should behave consistently across client instances.

expected: Natural prompts using product vocabulary are more likely to attach the correct tools without requiring exact MCP tool names.
The DreamGraph repository remains just another workspace from the product's perspective.
Some broad terms may attach scheduler tools more often, but this is acceptable when they are core product vocabulary and only affect tool availability, not automatic execution.
risks: Broad keyword matching can increase the number of attached tools for prompts that mention DreamGraph without scheduling intent.
Future contributors may reintroduce repository-specific assumptions when testing DreamGraph on itself.

guard_rails: Do not use the current repository name or product self-hosting context as a reason to suppress generic product keywords.
Keep prompt-routing changes advisory: attaching a tool group must not execute tools automatically.
Prefer focused routing tests that include both generic client projects and the DreamGraph repository as equivalent workspaces.

decisions.title: Standalone Architect migration is plan-centered and daemon-authoritative

context.problem: The standalone Architect migration needs a DreamGraph-specific implementation plan rather than a generic browser IDE plan. The plan must bind to accepted ADRs, preserve graph-first/daemon-authoritative practices, and clarify how plans, ADRs, AFE, scheduler operations, and governed mutations become standalone browser workflows.
constraints: DreamGraph remains local-first and daemon-authoritative; browser clients do not gain direct filesystem or graph mutation authority.
Accepted ADRs for tool priority, Explorer consistency/mutation safety, task/card persistence, context authority, AFE advisory semantics, product vocabulary, and VS Code canonicality remain binding.
Current VS Code V1 hybrid ChatPanel remains the canonical extension surface until a superseding ADR changes that boundary.
Implementation planning must follow ADR-142: Markdown plan for human narrative and ADR mirror for machine-readable graph reasoning.
Standalone Architect should become a graph-grounded implementation orchestrator centered on explicit plans, not a generic AI IDE or editor-first chat surface.

decision.chosen: Adopt the revised plans/STANDALONE_ARCHITECT_MIGRATION_PLAN.md as the narrative implementation plan for migrating Architect into a standalone daemon-served browser control plane. The plan makes implementation plans first-class working objects, binds work to accepted ADR guard rails, routes execution and mutations through daemon/MCP governance, reuses Explorer-style snapshot/SSE/mutation safety semantics, surfaces AFE and scheduler operations as DreamGraph-native plan workflows, and keeps VS Code as a companion/escape-hatch surface until an explicit cutover ADR supersedes the current canonical VS Code decision.

alternatives.option: Treat standalone Architect as a generic browser IDE with direct file/editor operations
alternatives.rejected_because: This would violate DreamGraph's daemon-authoritative, graph-first, curated mutation, and audit/governance model.

alternatives.option: Only move the existing VS Code chat UI into a browser shell
alternatives.rejected_because: That would preserve chat as the primary abstraction and miss the core DreamGraph realization that plans are the primary operational object.

alternatives.option: Implement browser mutation endpoints before locking ADR bindings and safety model
alternatives.rejected_because: Mutation authority is the most sensitive boundary; Explorer and tool-priority ADRs require curated, audited, authenticated daemon-mediated flows.

alternatives.option: Replace VS Code immediately during standalone work
alternatives.rejected_because: ADR-192 keeps the V1 hybrid VS Code ChatPanel as the canonical extension surface until a superseding ADR/cutover is recorded.

expected: Future standalone Architect work has a DreamGraph-specific implementation roadmap with phases, API/data ownership assumptions, guard rails, and verification criteria.
Plan work can be queried by the graph through this ADR while the Markdown file remains the human-readable narrative source.

Implementation slices will start from daemon API skeleton, plan registry/graph binding, SPA shell, execution trace projection, mutation review, AFE/scheduler integration, VS Code compatibility, and release hardening.
Reviewers can check proposed standalone changes against explicit ADR bindings before code is written.
risks: The plan is still pre-implementation and exact endpoint/type names may change during design.
Some existing Explorer/Architect internals may not map cleanly to the proposed phased boundaries without adapter work.
Additional ADRs are still required for concrete API contracts, persistence schema, mutation review semantics, and VS Code cutover behavior.

guard_rails: Do not implement standalone browser filesystem writes or arbitrary graph mutations; route through daemon-governed intents and MCP tools.
Do not bypass the established MCP-first tool priority or omit fallback justifications in standalone execution flows.
Do not make AFE a hard enforcement mechanism without a new ADR; keep it advisory and subordinate to accepted ADR/API/workflow constraints.
Do not activate or deprecate VS Code Architect paths without a superseding ADR that addresses ADR-192.
Do not start implementation slices that change architecture boundaries without updating both the Markdown plan and ADR mirror per ADR-142.

decisions.title: Defend graph purity by separating durable plans from adaptive operational graph cognition

context.problem: Standalone Architect plans and implementation slices need permanent historical preservation, but completed workflow/task cognition must not remain indefinitely active in the DreamGraph. If every completed task, slice, checkpoint, and execution instruction stayed in the active graph forever, retrieval and reasoning would accumulate stale context and the underlying LLM would drown in obsolete operational detail instead of seeing current project reality.
constraints: Markdown plans under plans/ are durable project artifacts and must remain preserved after completion.
Per-plan implementation logs are mandatory for auditability, user visibility, and crash/power-outage recovery.
The DreamGraph prioritizes active project understanding, durable operational state, accepted architecture, verified capabilities, and current implementation reality.
Temporary execution workflow structures are useful during active implementation but become harmful when they continue to participate in active cognition after stabilization.
Historical evidence must remain available through markdown plans, implementation logs, ADR history, provenance, and archived evidence even when temporary graph workflow entities fade.
Graph RAG and Architect context assembly must avoid overloading the LLM with stale completed-task context.

decision.chosen: Plans remain as permanent markdown-backed historical artifacts, while graph workflow cognition is adaptive and temporary. During active work, plans may be operationalized into graph workflow entities such as plan nodes, slice nodes, gates, continuation state, checkpoints, candidate futures, and execution entities. As work completes and stabilizes, those temporary structures must crystallize into durable project knowledge by creating, mutating, enriching, superseding, merging into, or removing durable entities such as Feature, DataModel, Workflow, API, Capability, Tool, UIRegistryElement, ADR, and related project-state entities. Completed implementation instructions should not remain indefinitely active as future execution cognition.

alternatives.option: Keep every plan, task, slice, checkpoint, and implementation step permanently active in the graph.
alternatives.rejected_because: This preserves detail but pollutes operational cognition, increases stale retrieval, and risks drowning the LLM in obsolete execution context.

alternatives.option: Remove completed plans and logs once graph entities are updated.
alternatives.rejected_because: This destroys the permanent historical project record and undermines auditability, reasoning traceability, and crash/recovery continuity.

alternatives.option: Store plans only in the graph and not in markdown.
alternatives.rejected_because: This makes historical artifacts dependent on graph lifecycle policies and conflicts with DreamGraph markdown-backed planning practices.

alternatives.option: Never create temporary workflow graph entities for plans.
alternatives.rejected_because: This avoids graph cleanup but loses useful active coordination, review gates, continuation state, and graph-aware implementation support during execution.

expected: Plans and implementation logs remain permanently available under plans/ as historical evidence.
The active graph remains focused on current durable project reality instead of completed execution instructions.
Planning tools must distinguish temporary workflow state from durable project entities.
planning:sync_plan_graph and planning:archive_plan must support crystallization and fading of completed workflow cognition.
Graph RAG context quality should improve by avoiding retrieval of stale completed slices as if they were active work.
Users retain visibility into implemented vs unimplemented plan parts through markdown logs even after workflow graph structures are archived or removed.
risks: Crystallization bugs could remove useful workflow context before durable entities are correctly updated.
Over-aggressive graph cleanup could make resume behavior worse if implementation logs are incomplete.
Under-aggressive cleanup could still allow stale execution cognition to pollute retrieval.
Entity mapping from slices to durable graph concepts may require human review for ambiguous plans.

guard_rails: Do not delete or discard markdown plans or their implementation logs after completion.
Do not keep completed plan slices, checkpoints, or execution instructions indefinitely active in the graph once they have stabilized.
Before fading temporary workflow entities, crystallize verified results into durable project entities or record why no durable graph change is appropriate.
planning:archive_plan must preserve historical markdown artifacts and provenance while reducing active graph workflow noise.
planning:get_resume_packet must prefer the live implementation log and current durable project state over stale completed workflow entities.
Graph RAG and Architect context assembly should prioritize durable project entities and active plan state, not archived completed-task cognition.
Any implementation that treats the graph as the sole historical store for plans violates this decision.

decisions.title: Standalone Architect API uses a versioned daemon-governed /api/architect contract

context.problem: The standalone Architect migration needs a concrete API boundary before implementation begins. Without an explicit ADR, route naming, plan/run payloads, event streaming, and execution authority could drift between browser, daemon, and VS Code surfaces.
constraints: Standalone Architect is daemon-authoritative per ADR-206; the browser issues governed intents and does not gain direct filesystem or graph mutation authority.

Explorer consistency and mutation-safety semantics from ADR-087 remain binding: snapshot-first reads, live events, replay-gap recovery, curated mutation endpoints, audit context, and optimistic concurrency where applicable.
The API must support plan listing, plan detail, run/task visibility, review-gate decisions, and live updates without making exact v0 field names prematurely rigid.
Future endpoint names may evolve, but the versioned namespace and governed-intent boundary must stay stable.

decision.chosen: Lock the standalone Architect transport boundary to a daemon-served, versioned `/api/architect/*` contract plus the `/architect` app shell. The browser may list plans, inspect a plan with graph bindings, trigger governed slice/gate intents, inspect run/pass/task state, and subscribe to an Architect event stream, but it does so only through daemon-owned contracts that preserve Explorer-style snapshot/event consistency and governed mutation semantics.

alternatives.option: Expose standalone Architect through ad hoc unversioned daemon routes and payloads
alternatives.rejected_because: This weakens forward-compatibility and makes browser/daemon contracts drift-prone during phased implementation.

alternatives.option: Let the browser call existing lower-level tools or filesystem-like routes directly
alternatives.rejected_because: This violates the daemon-governed intent boundary and would bypass audit and mutation safety expectations.

alternatives.option: Postpone the contract decision until after UI work begins
alternatives.rejected_because: That would allow early implementation slices to hard-code unstable route and event assumptions.

expected: Phase 1 can implement an API skeleton without re-opening the authority boundary.
Browser and VS Code companion surfaces can converge on one plan/run contract instead of inventing separate orchestration APIs.
Replay-gap, stale-state, and audit behaviors inherit established Explorer-style expectations rather than becoming implicit UI behavior.
risks: Early field choices may still require additive evolution as implementation clarifies run and review payloads.
Some Explorer semantics may need adapter shaping for plan/run concepts rather than graph-only concepts.

guard_rails: Do not add standalone Architect endpoints outside a versioned `/api/architect` namespace unless they are static asset routes for `/architect` itself.
Do not let browser clients bypass daemon-governed intents for plan execution, review gates, or mutations.
Do not treat the live event stream as authoritative without snapshot/bootstrap and replay-gap recovery behavior.
Do not make exact route names or payload fields a reason to violate the stable authority boundary established here.

decisions.title: Standalone Architect plan operational state is daemon-owned and crystallizes into durable graph knowledge

context.problem: The migration plan required a decision on where active plan state lives. Without an explicit rule, implementation could fragment state across sidecar JSON, browser-local business state, markdown-only mutation, or permanently-active graph execution structures.
constraints: ADR-142 requires markdown plan narrative plus ADR/graph-readable mirrors, not markdown alone.
ADR-207 requires permanent markdown preservation while keeping active graph cognition adaptive and temporary.
Current slice, status, checkpoints, gate outcomes, continuation state, run traces, and pending review state need daemon-owned coordination so resume behavior survives browser reloads and UI restarts.
UI-local state such as layout, focus, and selection may remain browser-local, but durable operational state must remain authoritative in DreamGraph-owned records.

decision.chosen: Lock active standalone Architect plan state to daemon-owned DreamGraph operational records and graph workflow cognition during active execution, while preserving markdown plans and append-only implementation logs as the durable historical record. Active state may include current slice, status, checkpoints, gate decisions, continuation state, task/run traces, and pending review projections. As work stabilizes, temporary workflow cognition must crystallize into durable project entities or fade from active cognition per ADR-207.

alternatives.option: Persist active plan state primarily in browser storage or a frontend-only cache
alternatives.rejected_because: This breaks crash/reload continuity and makes the browser the accidental source of truth for operational state.

alternatives.option: Keep all plan state only in markdown files
alternatives.rejected_because: Markdown is the historical narrative record, not the sole coordination substrate for active plan execution and checkpoints.

alternatives.option: Keep completed execution structures permanently active in the graph
alternatives.rejected_because: ADR-207 rejects permanent active cognition for completed slices because it pollutes retrieval with stale execution detail.

expected: Resume packets and plan status can be reconstructed from daemon-owned operational records plus append-only markdown logs.
The browser stays a projection/control surface rather than a business-state owner.
Implementation can distinguish between historical plan artifacts and active coordination state without inventing sidecar persistence silos.
risks: Entity mapping from active slices to durable graph updates may still require careful implementation review.
If daemon-owned state and markdown logs drift, resume UX may become confusing until synchronization tooling matures.

guard_rails: Do not store authoritative active plan execution state exclusively in browser-local storage or frontend-only caches.
Do not treat markdown plans as the only operational state store for checkpoints, continuation, or review state.
Do not keep completed plan execution structures indefinitely active once their verified outcomes have crystallized into durable project entities.
Do not introduce a separate sidecar persistence model for core operational plan state unless a future ADR explicitly justifies it.

decisions.title: VS Code remains the companion Architect surface until a deliberate standalone cutover ADR

context.problem: The migration plan required a concrete coexistence and cutover decision for VS Code. Without it, implementation could drift into duplicated orchestration logic or accidentally deprecate the canonical VS Code path before standalone Architect is ready.
constraints: ADR-206 already states that VS Code remains a companion/escape-hatch surface until an explicit cutover ADR supersedes the current canonical boundary.
Phase 7 requires no duplicated orchestration logic between VS Code and standalone.
Standalone Architect must become a daemon-served browser control plane, but existing VS Code flows still need editing escape hatches and continuity during migration.
Any activation, deprecation, or thin-client transition must be deliberate and reviewable.
affected_entities: deep links between standalone and VS Code

decision.chosen: Lock the coexistence model so VS Code remains the companion Architect surface during migration, with standalone Architect becoming the daemon-served plan-first control plane and VS Code providing editing escape hatches, deep links, and eventual thin-client integration opportunities. No activation, deprecation, or cutover of the canonical VS Code path occurs until a dedicated superseding ADR explicitly defines the transition.

alternatives.option: Replace or deprecate VS Code Architect immediately as standalone work begins
alternatives.rejected_because: This would violate the accepted migration boundary and remove a working companion surface before the browser control plane is proven.

alternatives.option: Keep standalone and VS Code as permanently separate orchestration stacks
alternatives.rejected_because: This would duplicate logic, increase drift risk, and undermine the daemon-authoritative design.

alternatives.option: Decide cutover ad hoc in implementation PRs without a dedicated ADR
alternatives.rejected_because: That would make activation and deprecation behavior hard to audit and easy to change accidentally.

expected: Implementation can share daemon orchestration contracts across browser and VS Code without duplicating control logic.
Users retain a stable editing/escape-hatch surface while the standalone control plane matures.
Future cutover work has a clear review trigger instead of happening by drift.
risks: Maintaining two user-facing surfaces during migration adds integration overhead.
Delay in recording a future cutover ADR could prolong dual-surface complexity.

guard_rails: Do not duplicate core orchestration logic between VS Code and standalone Architect.
Do not deactivate, deprecate, or silently thin-client the VS Code Architect surface without a dedicated superseding ADR.
Do not make standalone-only assumptions that remove VS Code deep-link and escape-hatch interoperability during migration.

decisions.title: Standalone Architect mutation review is a curated audited Keep-Undo review workflow

context.problem: The migration plan required an exact mutation review contract for daemon-produced patches reviewed from the browser. Without an explicit decision, browser mutation flows could blur together direct edits, opaque approvals, or unaudited reverts.
constraints: Browser clients do not gain direct filesystem authority; daemon-mediated mutation tools and governed intents remain authoritative per ADR-206 and ADR-144.
ADR-087 requires curated mutation flows, audit context, and concurrency visibility rather than arbitrary writes.
The UI needs explicit review actions for daemon-produced diffs and must surface ADR guard-check warnings before governed mutation.
Fallbacks to non-MCP or non-preferred paths must remain visible and justified.

decision.chosen: Lock standalone Architect mutation review to a curated diff workflow where the daemon proposes or stages changes, the browser renders pending diffs and guard-rail warnings, and the user-facing review actions remain explicit and auditable. `Keep` means accept and retain the governed daemon-produced mutation outcome. `Undo` means discard or revert the pending outcome through daemon-governed reversal semantics rather than direct browser file writes. Review decisions, reasons, and guard-check visibility are part of the durable audit trail.

alternatives.option: Let the browser directly edit files and save accepted patches
alternatives.rejected_because: This bypasses daemon governance, auditability, and the established mutation authority model.

alternatives.option: Auto-apply daemon-produced patches without an explicit review contract
alternatives.rejected_because: This hides risk and weakens the user's ability to inspect or reject mutations before they land.

alternatives.option: Treat Keep and Undo as informal UI labels without durable audit semantics
alternatives.rejected_because: That would make review outcomes ambiguous and hard to reason about during resume, rollback, and provenance analysis.

expected: Phase 5 can implement a safe browser review loop without inventing ad hoc mutation semantics.
Resume behavior can explain which diffs are pending, accepted, or undone with durable audit evidence.
Review UX stays compatible with ADR guard-check surfacing and tool-tier fallback visibility.
risks: Exact revert mechanics may still need implementation detail work for multi-file or partially accepted changes.
Users may expect broader git-style history operations than the initial governed Keep/Undo scope supports.

guard_rails: Do not let the browser accept, edit, or revert code changes through direct filesystem authority.
Do not hide ADR guard-check warnings or audit reasons when presenting daemon-produced mutations for review.
Do not implement silent mutation application or silent revert behavior for standalone Architect review flows.
Do not normalize non-MCP fallback mutation paths as routine; they must remain visible and justified.

decisions.title: Standalone Architect browser access reuses DreamGraph instance auth and local-first remote-access semantics

context.problem: The migration plan required an auth-boundary decision for browser mutation and review flows. Without a decision, standalone Architect could drift toward bespoke identity infrastructure, weak unaudited mutation access, or remote-access assumptions that conflict with DreamGraph's local-first model.
constraints: DreamGraph remains local-first per the migration plan's Remote Access Philosophy.

Remote access is expected through secure tunnel or reverse proxy patterns such as VS Code port forwarding, Cloudflare Tunnel, Tailscale, ngrok, or SSH reverse proxy, not through a new DreamGraph identity platform.
Mutation review and execution flows must preserve instance isolation, audit semantics, and existing daemon authentication expectations.
Standalone Architect must distinguish authenticated mutation capability from read-only or stale-state visibility.

decision.chosen: Lock standalone Architect access control to existing DreamGraph instance-authenticated daemon semantics, preserving the distinction between daemon-served browser access and governed mutation authority. Remote access remains local-first and operator-mediated through secure tunnel or reverse-proxy patterns rather than a new DreamGraph identity product. Mutation, review, and execution routes must require authenticated instance-scoped access and preserve audit/isolation semantics; browser convenience must not outrank these protections.

alternatives.option: Build a new first-party DreamGraph identity and session product as part of standalone Architect
alternatives.rejected_because: This expands scope away from graph cognition and orchestration and duplicates infrastructure better handled by operator-selected access layers.

alternatives.option: Allow mutation flows over unauthenticated or read-equivalent browser access
alternatives.rejected_because: This would violate instance isolation and mutation audit expectations.

alternatives.option: Treat remote access as unsupported so the browser surface remains effectively localhost-only
alternatives.rejected_because: The plan explicitly allows secure remote access through operator-controlled tunnels and proxies.

expected: Implementation can reuse existing auth/isolation semantics instead of inventing a separate identity stack.
Remote browser access remains possible without redefining DreamGraph as a hosted auth platform.
Mutation endpoints can inherit clear authentication expectations from existing daemon/Explorer patterns.
risks: Legacy or minimally configured deployments may still have weaker auth postures and need explicit operator guidance.
Users may expect more polished remote-auth UX than the initial operator-mediated approach provides.

guard_rails: Do not expand standalone Architect into a new DreamGraph identity-platform scope without a dedicated ADR.
Do not allow governed mutation, review, or execution flows on unauthenticated or insufficiently scoped browser access.
Do not weaken instance isolation or audit requirements for the sake of remote convenience.
Do not describe standalone Architect as a hosted multi-tenant web product when the architecture remains local-first and daemon-served.

decisions.title: Standalone Architect Adaptive Future Engine review records stay advisory, provenance-rich, and supersession-aware

context.problem: The migration plan required a durable review schema for plan-bound Adaptive Future Engine outputs. Without an explicit ADR, candidate futures, review decisions, provenance, and supersession handling could be inconsistently modeled or mistaken for hard enforcement.
constraints: ADR-204 makes the Adaptive Future Engine advisory and explicitly forbids hard enforcement without new ADR review.
ADR-203 model-routing order and fallback visibility remain binding for LLM-enabled AFE work.

The plan already requires AFE plan surfaces to show candidate futures, future-fit score and evidence, future objections, prior outcomes, model provenance/fallback reason, human review decisions, and supersession/review status.
Plan-bound future records need to support historical review and active decisioning without polluting durable project truth as if speculative futures were accepted architecture.

decision.chosen: Lock AFE plan review records to a provenance-rich, advisory schema that at minimum captures: candidate future identity, future-fit score and evidence, future objections, known prior future outcomes, model provenance, fallback reason when applicable, human review decision, review timestamp/actor context, and supersession status or replacement linkage. These records inform planning and review, but they do not become hard constraints or durable accepted architecture unless separately crystallized into ADRs or other durable project entities after review.

alternatives.option: Treat AFE output as an implicit ranking with no durable review record
alternatives.rejected_because: This loses provenance, decision history, and supersession context for plan-bound futures.

alternatives.option: Promote winning futures directly into hard enforcement or accepted truth without review
alternatives.rejected_because: ADR-204 forbids turning AFE into a hard enforcement mechanism without separate governance.

alternatives.option: Store only a free-text note about future recommendations
alternatives.rejected_because: That would make provenance, decision status, and supersession semantics too ambiguous for operational use.

expected: Standalone Architect can render explainable future-review UI without confusing advisory rankings for accepted truth.
Future records can be compared, superseded, and resumed across plan work with clear provenance.
AFE implementation remains aligned with advisory governance instead of drifting toward hidden enforcement.
risks: The initial schema may need additive fields as real review workflows expose missing nuance.
Users may still over-trust scored futures unless the UI clearly distinguishes advisory signals from accepted decisions.

guard_rails: Do not treat AFE candidate futures or scores as hard blockers or accepted architecture without separate reviewed crystallization.
Do not omit model provenance, fallback reason, or supersession state from durable future-review records.
Do not let AFE review UX hide future objections or prior outcome evidence when available.
Do not collapse human review decisions into opaque score-only outcomes.

decisions.title: Standalone Architect runtime identity is a daemon-owned session object

context.problem: Standalone Architect previously assembled adapter, provider, model, autonomy, top-bar labels, chat route context, trace metadata, and provenance from separate UI and daemon fields. That allowed selector state, actual runtime state, and assistant prompt context to diverge, making model identity unreliable as governance metadata during native API, Codex CLI, Copilot CLI, deterministic fallback, and audit flows.
constraints: Model identity is governance metadata and must be available to UI, prompt context, traces, and provenance from one authoritative object.
Browser selectors may mutate runtime state only through daemon-governed POST endpoints and persisted engine.env keys; they must not become an independent source of truth.
CLI adapters remain intermediate execution routes, not native API providers, so adapter identity and provider identity must both be represented.
Runtime identity must not expose secrets or raw prompt content.
ADR-206/ADR-210 daemon-served standalone Architect boundaries and ADR-201 native CLI adapter boundaries remain binding.

decision.chosen: Represent the active standalone Architect execution identity as a daemon-owned session runtime object containing adapter, provider, model, autonomy_mode, pass_state, execution_route, and session_id. Return this runtime in status/config/chat/future-review payloads, render the top bar from it, mutate it through the config endpoint, inject it into chat system context, and attach it to route, trace, and provenance metadata.

alternatives.option: Keep selector state, route metadata, and chat prompt metadata independently assembled.
alternatives.rejected_because: This preserves the mismatch that caused the UI to show one model while the assistant lacked reliable runtime identity.

alternatives.option: Treat the provider/model selector as the source of truth in browser localStorage.
alternatives.rejected_because: Browser-local state is not authoritative governance metadata and can drift from engine.env and daemon execution.

alternatives.option: Collapse CLI adapters into provider values.
alternatives.rejected_because: Codex CLI and Copilot CLI are intermediate adapter routes, not native API providers; collapsing them would violate adapter/provider boundaries.

expected: Top-bar runtime labels, selector persistence, chat context, tool traces, and provenance refer to the same session runtime object.
The assistant can answer its current adapter/provider/model/session identity from injected runtime context instead of claiming uncertainty.
Runtime changes remain auditable through daemon payloads and engine.env persistence.
Future adapter work can attach richer execution details without changing the core runtime identity contract.
risks: The initial standalone runtime object is process-local and may need durable session lifecycle refinements later.
CLI adapter execution is still metadata-only in this standalone path until full CLI orchestration is ported.
Additional UI surfaces may need migration from legacy architect_llm aliases to runtime over time.

guard_rails: Do not make browser localStorage, selector DOM state, or chat request fields the authoritative runtime identity.
Do not let top-bar labels, prompt context, trace metadata, and provenance derive adapter/provider/model from different sources.
Do not collapse Codex CLI or Copilot CLI into native API provider values; keep adapter and provider separate.
Do not log secrets, raw prompts, or raw tool payloads as part of runtime identity.
Do not remove runtime identity from chat system context or provenance without an equivalent daemon-owned replacement.

decisions.title: Standalone Architect CLI adapters execute through a daemon MCP bridge

context.problem: Standalone Architect exposed Codex CLI and Copilot CLI selector options, but the chat route treated those selections as metadata-only fallback. That violated the adapter/runtime identity model and prevented selected CLI adapters from using DreamGraph MCP tools as the authoritative repository operation path.
constraints: ADR-201 requires CLI adapters to be first-class DreamGraph Architect adapters rather than dumb metadata labels.
ADR-216 requires adapter, provider, model, runtime, traces, and provenance to agree on one daemon-owned session runtime.
CLI adapters must keep provider-native shell/read/write routes denied and route repository actions through DreamGraph MCP tools.
The browser must not become the authority for adapter execution or filesystem access.
Bridge startup must fail closed when the upstream daemon MCP endpoint cannot be reached or required tools are absent.

decision.chosen: Standalone Architect chat requests with adapter codex-cli or copilot-cli now invoke a daemon-owned CLI bridge. The bridge materializes per-run CLI home/config files, exposes the active daemon MCP endpoint to the selected CLI through a stdio MCP proxy, audits tool calls, and returns normalized content, route, provenance, and tool trace metadata. Metadata-only fallback is no longer used for selected CLI chat execution.

alternatives.option: Keep codex-cli and copilot-cli selector values as metadata-only deterministic fallbacks.
alternatives.rejected_because: That was the reported bug and made UI/runtime/provenance metadata claim an adapter path that was not actually used.

alternatives.option: Spawn a fresh DreamGraph stdio server directly for each CLI run.
alternatives.rejected_because: That can create a second graph/session boundary instead of using the active daemon session.

alternatives.option: Let CLI adapters use provider-native filesystem and shell tools for repository operations.
alternatives.rejected_because: That bypasses DreamGraph MCP authority and weakens auditability.

expected: Selecting Codex CLI or Copilot CLI in the standalone Architect launches the real CLI path for chat execution.
Selected CLI adapters receive DreamGraph MCP tools including run_command through the bridge instead of provider-native shell/write/read routes.
CLI runs emit route/provenance/tool trace metadata tied to the active Architect runtime.
If the daemon MCP endpoint or required tools are unavailable, the selected CLI path fails explicitly rather than pretending to be metadata-only success.
risks: CLI versions may change their argument/config semantics and require bridge updates.
The initial standalone bridge normalizes post-run tool audit records rather than fully streaming every CLI event into the browser.
Development-mode tsx bridge spawning may depend on the host process exec arguments until the compiled bridge exists.

guard_rails: Do not reintroduce metadata-only fallback for selected codex-cli or copilot-cli chat execution.
Do not let standalone CLI adapters answer repository questions without a reachable DreamGraph MCP bridge or an explicit fail-closed error.
Do not route CLI repository mutations through provider-native shell/write/read surfaces when DreamGraph MCP tools are available.
Do not spawn a separate graph-authority session for CLI runs without a new ADR that addresses active daemon runtime identity.
Keep CLI adapter route, runtime, provenance, and tool trace metadata synchronized with ADR-216.

decisions.title: Standalone Architect plan status separates lifecycle from execution state

context.problem: Standalone Architect plan status projection used a vague single status field and could let generic action_recorded checkpoints override durable implementation checkpoints, causing Browser Architect UI Level 2 to show unknown or stale current slice after completed work.
constraints: ADR-209 requires active plan operational state to be daemon-owned and reconstructable from operational records plus append-only implementation logs.
Planning and implementation are separate lifecycle concerns; UI must not collapse them into a vague in_progress or unknown status.
Generic chat/action audit entries are useful history but must not outrank concrete implementation slice checkpoints for current resume status.
Browser UI remains a projection surface and must refresh from daemon APIs after governed chat runs instead of owning authoritative status locally.

decision.chosen: Project standalone Architect plan state as distinct plan_lifecycle and execution_state fields, with last_completed_slice, next_slice, active_slice, and active_phase derived from daemon-owned implementation-log checkpoints. Concrete implementation checkpoints are preferred over generic action_recorded entries, and the browser refreshes the daemon plan projection after chat runs so status changes are visible without manual page reload.

alternatives.option: Continue displaying only plan.status/current_slice from the latest log heading.
alternatives.rejected_because: This kept Status unknown/in_progress and allowed generic action_recorded checkpoints to hide completed implementation slice progress.

alternatives.option: Let the browser infer current slice from visible plan text after a run.
alternatives.rejected_because: That would make the browser an authority for operational plan state, conflicting with ADR-209.

expected: Browser Architect can show Lifecycle implementing, Execution idle, Last completed Slice 1, and Next slice Slice 2 for Browser Architect UI Level 2 after Slice 1 completion.
Timeout or partial execution can be represented as execution_state timed_out or partial without corrupting plan_lifecycle.
Plan rail and detail chips refresh from daemon projections after chat runs.
risks: Implementation-log parsing still depends on checkpoint heading conventions; malformed logs may project less detail until parser support expands.
Existing consumers of plan.status may need migration to the richer operational_state fields.

guard_rails: Do not use a vague single in_progress status as the only plan state display.
Do not let generic action_recorded or chat-plan-update checkpoints override later concrete implementation checkpoints as current slice.
Do not make browser-local storage the source of truth for lifecycle, execution state, completed slice, or next slice.
Keep plan_lifecycle and execution_state distinct in daemon payloads and UI labels.

decisions.title: Standalone Architect chat scope separates project prompts from plan execution

context.problem: Standalone browser Architect chat previously treated a selected plan as implicit context for every prompt, causing global project/repo/graph questions to inherit selected-plan context and risk polluting selected-plan implementation logs or planning action records.
constraints: Standalone Architect remains daemon-authoritative and browser clients only send governed intents through /api/architect/v1 per ADR-208.
Plan operational state and implementation logs remain durable daemon-owned records per ADR-209 and ADR-218.
Users need a valid no-plan-selected state, and that state must imply Project chat scope.
Project-scope prompts can still use DreamGraph MCP tools and governed mutation authority, but project scope must not become an unsafe bypass mode.

decision.chosen: Add an explicit Architect chat scope contract with plan and project values. Plan scope binds prompts to the selected plan and may use selected-plan context/resume/log updates when the action is plan-related. Project scope treats prompts as global project/repo/graph requests, does not inject selected-plan context, and does not write selected-plan implementation-log or planning action records by default. The browser sends scope in /api/architect/v1/chat, supports /ask, /global, /repo, and /plan slash overrides, exposes a scope pill before send, and allows clearing the selected plan by clicking it again.

alternatives.option: Keep selected plans as implicit chat context for every prompt.
alternatives.rejected_because: This makes global graph/repo questions dirty plan execution context and implementation logs.

alternatives.option: Use separate chat pages for plan and project questions.
alternatives.rejected_because: That would fragment the standalone Architect workflow and duplicate route/UI behavior instead of making scope explicit in the existing governed contract.

alternatives.option: Let the browser infer whether a prompt is plan-related from assistant text after the run.
alternatives.rejected_because: The daemon/orchestrator must decide context injection and log-writing before execution; post-hoc inference cannot prevent pollution.

expected: Browser Architect can ask graph health or repo questions in Project scope without creating selected-plan implementation-log entries.
Plan-scoped slice execution continues to include selected plan context and use durable implementation-log checkpoints.
No plan selected remains a first-class UI state and defaults chat to Project scope.
Slash commands provide fast per-message override while preserving daemon-governed mutation rules.
risks: Users may expect the selected plan to remain active while the chat pill is in Project scope, so the UI must keep the scope label visible before send.
Some older clients that omit scope still rely on compatibility defaults based on whether a plan id is sent.
Future tool mutations in Project scope still require careful governance messaging so project scope is not mistaken for unrestricted mode.

guard_rails: Do not inject selected-plan context into Project-scope chat unless the user explicitly changes to Plan scope or a future ADR defines a narrower explicit-request contract.
Do not write selected-plan implementation-log entries or planning action records for Project-scope chat by default.
Do not force-select the first plan when no selected plan is configured or requested.
Do not make browser-local state the authority for plan execution; persist selected-plan changes through daemon-owned engine.env/Architect selection routes.

decisions.title: Architect Level 3 Slice 5 execution control implementation verified against binding ADRs

context.problem: Architect Level 3 Slice 5 needed a durable graph record that its task execution control implementation was verified against the binding ADR set after source inspection and DreamGraph-run verification, without duplicating already-applied source changes.
constraints: Slice 5 execution controls must remain daemon-normalized state transitions exposed through /api/architect/v1/commands rather than browser-local execution.
Runtime identity, route metadata, provenance, and CLI adapter behavior must stay synchronized with ADR-216 and ADR-217.
Prompt-bearing chat transport must remain POST-only per ADR-215; execution control commands must not introduce GET prompt leakage.
Plan lifecycle and execution state must remain distinct per ADR-218, and Project scope must not write selected-plan logs by default per ADR-219.
Raw CLI commands and raw CLI output must remain hidden from primary chat UX; structured formatted payloads are the user-facing contract.

decision.chosen: Treat the existing Architect Level 3 Slice 5 implementation as verified: runtime metadata exposes normalized execution-control capabilities and active execution snapshots; /stop, /pause, /resume, and steering flow through daemon command envelopes; supported stop requests use daemon-owned abort signaling for CLI bridge child processes; browser controls remain a projection of daemon state and keep raw CLI details out of normal chat output.

alternatives.option: Re-implement Slice 5 despite the implementation log and tests showing it is already applied.
alternatives.rejected_because: That would risk duplicate or divergent execution-control semantics without evidence of a missing source delta.

alternatives.option: Record only a chat summary without a graph decision.
alternatives.rejected_because: The user explicitly requested graph recording, and future guard-rail checks need durable graph context.

alternatives.option: Treat ADR guard warnings as conflicts and halt despite tests passing.
alternatives.rejected_because: The warnings were boundary reminders; source inspection showed the implementation satisfies daemon authority, POST transport, runtime identity, and scope separation constraints.

expected: Future graph queries can find the verified Slice 5 execution-control implementation and its source/test anchors.
Later Slice 6 UI work can build on the existing daemon execution-control contract instead of redefining stop, pause, resume, or steering semantics.
ADR guard checks have a durable reconciliation point tying Slice 5 to ADR-215, ADR-216, ADR-217, ADR-218, and ADR-219.
risks: Pause, resume, and steering are currently capability-gated false for CLI runtimes, so future provider support will require additive implementation and tests.
The record is verification-oriented and should not be mistaken for a new execution-control ADR that supersedes existing binding decisions.
Implementation-log parsing and active runtime snapshots remain sensitive to future route refactors.

guard_rails: Do not make browser buttons or slash parsing authoritative for execution state; they must call daemon command endpoints and render daemon snapshots.
Do not expose raw CLI commands or raw child-process output as the primary execution-control chat response.
Do not enable pause, resume, or steering for an adapter until the runtime can preserve and resume execution context with tests.
Do not reintroduce selected-plan implementation-log writes for Project-scope execution-control chatter by default.
Do not bypass the CLI MCP bridge or DreamGraph MCP authority when routing CLI adapter repository operations.

decisions.title: Architect plugin plan state is daemon-owned, namespaced, and action-mediated

context.problem: Architect plugin tabs need durable plan-bound state such as checklist items without making browser storage, selected-plan inference, or plan markdown a second authority.
constraints: Plan-bound reads and writes require explicit planId.
Plan state is persisted under daemon-owned instance data.
Writes must pass capability, effect, schema, plan existence, and revision checks.
Unload must remove active behavior while preserving persisted user state.

decision.chosen: Persist Architect plugin state per instance, plugin id, plan id, tab type id, and key in a daemon-owned JSON store using atomic writes and locking. Reads return immutable snapshots with revision tokens. Writes occur only through registered host-side plugin action handlers after capability, effect, schema, explicit plan existence, and revision checks. Project-scope summaries are exposed only when explicitly declared and never silently bind to a selected plan.

alternatives.option: Use browser localStorage as checklist authority
alternatives.rejected_because: Browser-local state would diverge across reloads and clients and bypass daemon governance.

alternatives.option: Write checklist toggles directly into plan markdown
alternatives.rejected_because: The initial slice needs namespaced operational plugin state, not implicit mutation of governed plan documents.

alternatives.option: Infer a target from the selected or first plan
alternatives.rejected_because: No selected plan is a valid state and implicit plan targeting violates plan-scope separation.

expected: Checklist state survives browser reload and plugin unload/reload.
State is isolated across plugins, plans, tabs, and keys.
Stale concurrent writes fail explicitly.
risks: A persistent store adds locking and migration concerns.
Plugins may need clear handling for missing plans and stale revisions.

guard_rails: Do not make browser localStorage authoritative for Architect plugin state, badges, or sidebar summaries.
Do not write checklist toggles directly into plan markdown in the initial implementation.
Do not target an implicit first plan or stale selected plan.
Do not delete persisted Architect plugin state during normal unload or reload.

decisions.title: Architect plugin capabilities extend the existing manifest trust envelope

context.problem: Architect plugin tabs need registration, plan reads, plan-state writes, and sidebar summaries while preserving the shipped plugin SDK trust, manifest, capability, effect, telemetry, and lifecycle model.
constraints: Architect extensions remain normal trusted DreamGraph plugins.
The existing plugin.json manifest and engine.dreamgraph compatibility check remain authoritative.
Every registration and invocation must be capability- and effect-gated, namespaced, telemetered, and removable on unload.
Architect tab registration does not imply repository mutation authority.

decision.chosen: Extend the existing SDK manifest additively with architect:register_tab, architect:read_plan, architect:write_plan_state, and architect:register_sidebar_summary capabilities plus render_architect_tab, read_architect_plan_projection, write_architect_plan_state, and render_architect_sidebar_summary effects. Gate and telemetry-record every Architect registration and invocation under the existing trusted plugin host lifecycle.

alternatives.option: Create a second privileged Architect plugin manifest or loader
alternatives.rejected_because: A parallel plugin class would duplicate trust and lifecycle rules and create drift.

alternatives.option: Allow Architect registration without capability or effect declarations
alternatives.rejected_because: That would bypass the SDK's explicit authority model and observability contract.

expected: Architect tabs compose with existing discovery, validation, trust banners, telemetry, unload, and reload behavior.
Static declarations can be checked before host registration is accepted.
Existing SDK clients remain compatible because the extension is additive.
risks: Capability drift can occur if manifests, host gates, reject reasons, and docs are not changed together.
New telemetry paths need focused regression tests.

guard_rails: Do not bypass plugin.json, engine.dreamgraph compatibility, trusted loading, capability checks, effect checks, reject reasons, or telemetry.
Do not create a privileged Architect plugin class outside the existing host runtime.
Do not treat Architect tab registration as repository mutation authority.
Keep SDK changes additive to the shipped plugin baseline.

decisions.title: Architect plugin browser API is a versioned daemon projection

context.problem: Standalone Architect needs to list contributed tabs, read plan-bound snapshots, and dispatch actions without embedding active plugin modules in the browser or exposing direct storage authority.
constraints: Browser clients use versioned /api/architect/v1 daemon contracts.
Actions are structured POST commands dispatched through active host registration.
Sidebar summaries and badges derive from the same validated snapshot contract.
Browser payloads must not reveal state-store paths or direct file APIs.

decision.chosen: Expose host-validated Architect plugin descriptors and explicit plan-bound snapshots through versioned /api/architect/v1 routes. Browser actions post structured commands to the daemon, which validates and dispatches to registered host-side handlers and returns a fresh snapshot. Sidebar summaries and badges are derived from that daemon snapshot.

alternatives.option: Bundle active plugin modules into the browser
alternatives.rejected_because: That would execute plugin code in a new trust domain and bypass the declarative host-rendered boundary.

alternatives.option: Expose store paths or direct file APIs to browser code
alternatives.rejected_because: That would leak implementation details and create browser-side mutation authority.

alternatives.option: Let browser actions call plugin handlers directly
alternatives.rejected_because: Actions must pass daemon routing, registration, scope, and schema checks.

expected: Browser rendering remains a projection over daemon-owned state.
Action failure cases can be represented as explicit HTTP responses.
Sidebar, badge, and tab content stay consistent because they share one snapshot contract.
risks: Route-file complexity may grow and require extraction.
Snapshot contract versioning must remain stable as renderer kinds expand.

guard_rails: Do not embed active plugin modules into the browser bundle.
Do not expose raw state-store paths or direct file APIs.
Do not allow browser actions to bypass host registration, schema validation, or explicit plan scope.
Keep Architect plugin routes under the versioned daemon API contract.

decisions.title: Normalize LLM provider results and gate model parameters through capabilities

context.problem: Responses API output shapes and model-specific parameter support can change independently of DreamGraph's engine and Architect workflows. Direct reads of provider response objects and scattered model heuristics make GPT-5.x migrations brittle, especially for temperature and Responses API parsing.
constraints: DreamGraph must consume provider-normalized LLM results, not raw OpenAI Responses objects.
GPT-5.5 OpenAI calls must treat temperature as unsupported and optional.
Existing Chat Completions models such as gpt-5.4 must keep working without provider-id split.
ADR-147 and ADR-148 already require ModelCapabilities-driven routing and request shaping.

decision.chosen: Keep provider raw response parsing inside the OpenAI adapter boundary. Expose normalized result data with text, finishReason, and usage. Centralize daemon-side model parameter support in getModelCapabilities so request builders consult capabilities before sending optional parameters such as temperature.

alternatives.option: Continue extracting response.output/output_text at each DreamGraph call site
alternatives.rejected_because: It leaks OpenAI Responses schema details into orchestration code and makes schema evolution a behavioral risk.

alternatives.option: Preserve temperature as a required field for all OpenAI-compatible models
alternatives.rejected_because: GPT-5.5 does not expose temperature and model support must be negotiated as a capability.

alternatives.option: Infer GPT-5.x behavior from scattered regexes at each call site
alternatives.rejected_because: Duplicated heuristics drift and contradict ADR-147/ADR-148 capability-driven provider design.

expected: DreamGraph call sites depend on normalized LLM output shape instead of Responses API internals.
OpenAI request bodies omit temperature when the selected model capability does not support it.
Future model upgrades update one capability table instead of several call sites.
Determinism expectations remain documented as Normalizer/evidence/promotion behavior rather than a temperature guarantee.
risks: The daemon capability table still needs upkeep when providers publish new model behavior.
OpenAI Responses tool-loop migration remains a separate compatibility concern if daemon native tool calls are routed to Responses-only models.

guard_rails: Do not read OpenAI Responses output_text/output[]/status/incomplete_details outside the OpenAI adapter normalization boundary.
Do not send temperature or other optional parameters without checking model capabilities.
Do not add new GPT-5.x regex heuristics at call sites when a ModelCapabilities entry can express the behavior.
Do not treat low temperature as DreamGraph's determinism contract; the Normalizer, evidence scoring, and promotion gates remain the deterministic control surface.

decisions.title: Implementation status requires verified executable behavior, not plan/graph/doc updates

context.problem: Project status can become misleading if plan updates, graph edits, documentation changes, or scope changes are described as implemented before corresponding executable behavior exists and has been verified. This creates drift between DreamGraph facts, project documentation, and the actual source code.
constraints: Implementation claims must be grounded in actual executable source changes, not only metadata or narrative changes.
Graph facts must describe the current implementation state rather than aspirational or planned state.
Documentation and planning artifacts may describe intent, scope, or decisions, but they do not by themselves change runtime behavior.
Verification evidence is required before marking behavior as implemented.

decision.chosen: Treat plan, graph, documentation, and project-scope updates as non-implementation changes unless executable behavior changed in the source code and was verified. Implementation status may only be claimed after code-level changes exist and appropriate verification has passed or is explicitly documented. Graph updates must follow and reflect actual implementation state; graph changes alone are never sufficient evidence of implementation.

alternatives.option: Allow graph or documentation updates to mark functionality implemented
alternatives.rejected_because: This permits aspirational state to masquerade as runtime capability and causes drift between code, graph, and docs.

alternatives.option: Allow implementation claims based on unverified code changes
alternatives.rejected_because: Executable behavior may still be broken or incomplete; verification is part of the implementation evidence.

alternatives.option: Keep implementation status only in plans and not in graph
alternatives.rejected_because: DreamGraph uses graph state as project authority, so graph must remain aligned with code reality rather than disconnected from it.

expected: Implementation labels become more trustworthy and evidence-bound.
Plans, docs, and graph entries must distinguish intended, planned, in-progress, implemented, and verified states.
Graph maintenance must be synchronized with source-code reality and cannot be used as a shortcut around implementation.
Agents must avoid saying a task is implemented unless they can cite executable code changes and verification results.
risks: More conservative status reporting may slow perceived progress.
Some completed planning or graph hygiene work may need separate labels to avoid being mistaken for implementation.
Existing graph or plan entries may require cleanup if they previously overstated implementation state.

guard_rails: Do NOT mark a feature, workflow, remediation, or plan item as implemented solely because a plan, graph, documentation, ADR, or project-scope artifact changed.
Do NOT claim implementation unless executable project behavior changed in actual source code and verification evidence is available or explicitly recorded.
Do NOT let graph facts represent aspirational behavior as implemented; graph state must reflect actual implementation state.
Do NOT treat DreamGraph graph mutations, ADRs, living-doc exports, or scope metadata changes as sufficient implementation evidence.
When implementation status is ambiguous, label it as planned, documented, graph-recorded, or unverified rather than implemented.

decisions.title: Standalone Architect route boundary evidence is anchored on handleArchitectRoute

context.problem: The current API surface extraction missed the standalone Architect route symbol even though source inspection shows handleArchitectRoute is the exported daemon-owned HTTP boundary for /architect and /api/architect/v1. Future reasoning needs a durable anchor that this pass added curated API-surface evidence without claiming a new runtime implementation.
constraints: Implementation status must remain evidence-bound per ADR-234; this pass records evidence and API-surface curation, not a new executable feature.
Standalone Architect remains daemon-authoritative under ADR-206 and the versioned /api/architect contract under ADR-208.
Prompt-bearing chat transport, runtime identity, and plan/chat scope guard rails from ADR-215, ADR-216, and ADR-219 remain binding.
Curated API surface updates are allowed to correct stale extraction but must not supersede source-code verification.

decision.chosen: Treat src/architect/routes.ts::handleArchitectRoute as the current curated API-surface anchor for the standalone Architect daemon route boundary. Use source inspection and future API-surface refreshes to maintain the index; do not infer implementation changes from this evidence-only curation pass.

alternatives.option: Leave the stale/missing API-surface entry unrecorded
alternatives.rejected_because: Future graph/API-surface queries could continue to miss the canonical route function and force repeated rediscovery.

alternatives.option: Claim this pass implemented a new standalone Architect route feature
alternatives.rejected_because: No source behavior was changed; ADR-234 requires implementation claims to be grounded in executable source changes and verification.

expected: Future API-surface queries can find handleArchitectRoute even before a full extractor refresh.
Graph reasoning can link standalone_architect_daemon_routes to its source route function and binding ADR constraints.
The pass remains correctly classified as evidence/curation plus verification, not implementation.
risks: The hand-curated API-surface entry may drift if handleArchitectRoute is renamed or refactored without refreshing the index.
Additional route helper functions in src/architect/routes.ts may still be underrepresented until extraction is refreshed.

guard_rails: Do not treat curated API-surface entries as a substitute for source verification before behavior changes.
Do not claim route implementation status from graph/API-surface curation alone.
Refresh or recurate the API surface if handleArchitectRoute is renamed, split, or moved.
Keep standalone Architect route behavior constrained by ADR-208, ADR-215, ADR-216, and ADR-219 unless superseded.

decisions.title: Incremental reconciliation uses a journaled cross-store commit boundary

context.problem: Incremental scan must update multiple instance JSON stores without exposing a partially committed graph or allowing concurrent reconciliation to interleave.
constraints: Existing stores remain independent JSON files
atomicWriteFile guarantees one-file replacement only
Full scan remains recovery authority
Instance-aware locking must serialize reconciliation

decision.chosen: Use one instance-scoped reconciliation lease plus a durable write-ahead journal containing previous and next store bodies. Check the expected scan revision before commit, publish writes under the lease, remove the journal only after all writes succeed, and roll back from the journal on failure or daemon recovery.

alternatives.option: Immutable revision directories with an active pointer
alternatives.rejected_because: Requires all readers and data-path consumers to become revision-aware in one breaking migration.

alternatives.option: Best-effort independent atomic writes
alternatives.rejected_because: Can expose mixed old/new graph state and cannot safely recover after interruption.

expected: Concurrent incremental scans serialize
Revision conflicts fail safely
Interrupted commits are recoverable to the previous complete state
Existing store readers remain compatible
risks: Rollback cost scales with the bounded stores in one transaction
Readers not using the reconciliation barrier can observe a short commit window until migrated

guard_rails: Do NOT commit incremental multi-store mutations outside the reconciliation lease and journal.
Do NOT delete the journal before every store write succeeds.
Do NOT bypass expected-revision checks for incremental commits.
Full scan recovery must remain operational if incremental metadata is missing or incompatible.

decisions.title: Committed graph revisions are isolated by an instance read/write reconciliation barrier

context.problem: ADR-236's journaled rollback prevents durable partial commits but explicitly permits unbarriered readers to observe a mixed set while files are replaced. Slice 4 requires every externally observable graph read to see exactly one complete committed reconciliation revision.
constraints: Existing independent JSON stores and public JSON formats remain compatible
Readers must observe one committed graph revision, never a mixed old/new set
Full scan remains recovery authority
Critical-section performance is secondary to correctness for v1
Incremental authoritative reconciliation remains disabled until later slices

decision.chosen: Supersede ADR-236's reader-compatibility exception with a durable instance-level consistency policy: preview and staging remain outside the critical section; authoritative reconciliation acquires one exclusive graph barrier, revalidates the expected revision, journals prior and next bodies, replaces canonical stores, publishes scan_state.json last, invalidates caches, and releases only after success or complete rollback. Canonical multi-store readers hold the shared side for their entire snapshot. Ordinary enrichment, dream, scheduler, Architect/MCP, and manual atomic graph mutations use the exclusive side and cannot cross reconciliation.

alternatives.option: Immutable per-revision snapshot directories plus active pointer
alternatives.rejected_because: It would require a broader migration of all path consumers and persistence writers than Slice 4 needs; the centralized barrier proves the invariant without changing JSON locations.

alternatives.option: ADR-236 journal-only commit with scan_state publication last
alternatives.rejected_because: Rollback repairs disk but cannot retract a mixed snapshot already observed by an unbarriered reader.

alternatives.option: Ad-hoc scan locks at individual reader and mutation call sites
alternatives.rejected_because: Coverage would be fragile and legacy readers could bypass the contract; the common cache, snapshot, atomic-write, and reconciliation boundaries are narrower and coherent.

expected: Readers begun before commit finish on the prior complete revision
Readers arriving during commit wait and then see the new complete revision or restored prior revision
Canonical atomic mutations serialize against reconciliation
Interrupted journals roll back during recovery; rollback failure remains explicitly recovery_required
scan_state.json is the final publication write and caches are invalidated before readers resume
risks: Long multi-store reads can delay reconciliation and long commits can briefly delay reads
Direct legacy filesystem readers outside canonical graph APIs require explicit audit/migration before they may claim multi-store consistency
The barrier is daemon-process scoped; multiple independent daemon processes for one instance remain prohibited by the existing single-daemon ownership contract

guard_rails: Do NOT expose a canonical multi-store read without holding the shared graph barrier for the full snapshot.
Do NOT mutate canonical graph JSON outside the common atomic-write/mutation boundary.
Do NOT release the exclusive reconciliation barrier before cache invalidation and complete success or rollback.
Do NOT publish scan_state.json before every other transaction store replacement succeeds.
Do NOT clear a journal after rollback failure; preserve recovery_required state.
Do NOT enable authoritative incremental reconciliation until Slice 4 verification remains green.

decisions.title: Revision-scoped bridge discovery cache and bounded asynchronous audit evidence

context.problem: The external/Codex stdio-to-HTTP bridge duplicates tools/list during cold startup and synchronously appends complete tool results on the request hot path, producing measurable cold-path amplification and making large governed results vulnerable to audit backpressure.
constraints: Daemon MCP remains the sole repository and tool authority
Capabilities must not cross sessions or instances
MCP stdout must remain protocol-pure
Audit must retain correlation, ordering, failures, size and integrity evidence
Reconnect must invalidate cached discovery
ADR-050 keeps transport normalization silent; diagnostics belong at bridge operation boundaries

decision.chosen: Connect and initialize the upstream once, defer tools/list until the downstream client requests it, cache the result only for the lifetime of that upstream session, and invalidate it on upstream close. Move bridge audit writes to an ordered bounded buffer; store full small records but replace oversized input/result bodies with bounded previews plus byte size and SHA-256 hash. Flush within a bounded shutdown budget and surface overflow/write failure on stderr.

alternatives.option: Keep the eager startup probe and add a longer health timeout
alternatives.rejected_because: It preserves duplicate discovery and conceals rather than removes cold-path work.

alternatives.option: Persist a cross-session tool-list cache
alternatives.rejected_because: It risks stale capabilities and instance/session leakage without a daemon revision invalidation contract.

alternatives.option: Drop or sample audit records
alternatives.rejected_because: It weakens governed provenance and can silently omit security-relevant failures.

expected: Cold startup performs one initialize and at most one downstream-demanded discovery sequence
Warm tools/list calls avoid upstream round trips within one bridge session
Ordinary tool latency no longer waits for filesystem audit persistence
Large audit evidence has bounded memory/disk amplification while retaining integrity and provenance
risks: A server that mutates tools mid-session without reconnect will not be observed until cache invalidation
Buffered records may be lost if the process is forcibly terminated before bounded flush
Overflow handling must remain observable and preferentially preserve failures

guard_rails: Do NOT reuse discovery results across upstream sessions or instances.
Do NOT write operational diagnostics to MCP stdout.
Do NOT silently drop failed-call audit evidence.
Do NOT omit correlation id, duration, original byte size, and integrity hash when bounding audit bodies.
Do NOT automatically replay mutations after reconnect.

decisions.title: Layer-owned typed timeout and cancellation outcomes for governed CLI/MCP execution

context.problem: Stacked connect, discovery, queue, tool, idle, wall, and user-cancellation budgets could terminate one operation without identifying the owning layer or preserving correlation and retryability.
constraints: Daemon/MCP remains repository authority
Timeout increases must not conceal blocked transport
Cancellation must propagate upstream
Mutations must never be automatically replayed
Errors must retain correlation id, elapsed stage, tool and retryability

decision.chosen: Represent every deadline or cancellation as one typed outcome naming exactly one owner (connect, discovery, queue, tool, idle, wall, or user), propagate AbortSignal upstream, separate stage budgets, and make only explicitly transient layers retryable.

alternatives.option: Use one global wall timeout
alternatives.rejected_because: It cannot identify blocked stages and may terminate healthy long-running governed tools.

alternatives.option: Increase all existing timeout defaults
alternatives.rejected_because: It hides transport or progress failures and compounds stacked waiting.

alternatives.option: Allow each layer to report independent terminal failures
alternatives.rejected_because: Multiple owners make audit evidence ambiguous and risk orphan work.

expected: Timeout fixtures deterministically identify the owning layer
User cancellation aborts cooperative upstream work
Audit and CLI diagnostics can correlate a single terminal outcome
Connect/discovery budgets remain separate from tool execution
risks: Non-cooperative upstream operations may require subprocess termination after abort
Existing untyped call sites require incremental adoption
Retryability classification must remain conservative

guard_rails: Do NOT report more than one terminal owner for an operation.
